> Vengeance is mine; I will repay.
> — Romans 12:19, the novel’s epigraph
## Part One · Chapter I
All happy families are alike; each unhappy family is unhappy in its own way.

Everything was in confusion in the Oblonskys’ house. The wife had found out that the husband was having an affair with the French governess who used to live in their house, and she had announced to her husband that she could not go on living under the same roof with him. This state of things had now lasted for three days, and it was felt as a torment by the husband and wife themselves, by every member of the family, and by the whole household. Every member of the family and of the household felt that there was no sense in their living together, and that people who happen to meet at any wayside inn are more bound to one another than they, the family and household of the Oblonskys. The wife did not leave her rooms; the husband had not been home for three days. The children ran all over the house as if lost; the English governess had quarrelled with the housekeeper and written a note to a friend asking her to find her a new place; the cook had walked out of the yard the day before, at the very hour of dinner; the kitchen-maid and the coachman had asked for their wages.

On the third day after the quarrel, Prince Stepan Arkadyich Oblonsky, Stiva, as he was called in society, woke at his usual hour, that is, at eight o’clock in the morning, not in his wife’s bedroom but in his study, on the morocco-leather sofa. He turned his full, well-cared-for body over on the springs of the sofa, as though he wished to go back to sleep for a long while, hugged the pillow tightly from the other side and pressed his cheek to it; but suddenly he jumped up, sat on the sofa and opened his eyes.

“Yes, yes, how did it go?” he thought, remembering his dream. “Yes, how did it go? Yes! Alabin was giving a dinner in Darmstadt; no, not in Darmstadt, but something American. Yes, but Darmstadt was in America there. Yes, Alabin was giving a dinner on glass tables, yes, and the tables were singing Il mio tesoro, and not Il mio tesoro but something better, and there were some little decanters, and they were women too,” he remembered.

Stepan Arkadyich’s eyes shone merrily, and he sat thinking and smiling. “Yes, it was good, very good. There was a great deal more there that was excellent, only you can’t say it in words, and you can’t even put it into thoughts when you are awake.” And, noticing a strip of light that had made its way in at the side of one of the cloth blinds, he cheerfully swung his feet off the sofa, felt about with them for the slippers his wife had embroidered for him (a birthday present the year before), trimmed in gold morocco, and, by an old habit of nine years, without getting up, reached out his hand to the place where his dressing-gown hung in the bedroom. And then he suddenly remembered how and why he was sleeping not in his wife’s bedroom but in the study; the smile vanished from his face, and he wrinkled his forehead.

“Ah, ah, ah! Aaah!” he groaned, remembering everything that had happened. And all the details of the quarrel with his wife rose up again before his imagination, all the hopelessness of his position, and, most tormenting of all, his own guilt.

“Yes! She won’t forgive, and she can’t forgive. And the most terrible thing of all is that I am the cause of it all; I am the cause, and yet I am not to blame. That is where the whole drama lies,” he thought. “Ah, ah, ah!” he kept muttering in despair, remembering the impressions of the quarrel that were hardest for him to bear.

Most unpleasant of all had been that first minute when, coming home from the theatre, cheerful and pleased with himself, with a huge pear for his wife in his hand, he had not found his wife in the drawing-room; to his surprise had not found her in the study either; and at last had seen her in the bedroom, with the unlucky note that had revealed everything in her hand.

She, this Dolly, eternally anxious and fussing and not very clever, as he considered her, was sitting motionless with the note in her hand, and looking at him with an expression of horror, despair and anger.
“What is this? This?” she kept asking, pointing to the note.
And in this memory, as so often happens, what tormented Stepan Arkadyich was not so much the event itself as the way he had answered his wife’s words.

What happened to him at that minute is what happens to people when they are unexpectedly caught in something too shameful. He had not managed to prepare his face for the position he found himself in before his wife after the discovery of his guilt. Instead of taking offence, denying, justifying himself, begging forgiveness, even remaining indifferent (anything would have been better than what he did!), his face quite involuntarily (“reflexes of the brain,” thought Stepan Arkadyich, who was fond of physiology), quite involuntarily smiled all of a sudden its habitual, kindly and therefore foolish smile.

That foolish smile he could not forgive himself. Seeing it, Dolly shuddered as if from a physical pain, burst out, with the hot temper that was hers, into a torrent of cruel words, and ran out of the room. Since then she had refused to see her husband.
“That foolish smile is to blame for everything,” thought Stepan Arkadyich.
“But what is to be done? What is to be done?” he said to himself in despair, and found no answer.
## Chapter II

Stepan Arkadyich was a truthful man in his dealings with himself. He could not deceive himself and persuade himself that he repented of what he had done. He could not now repent of what he had repented of some six years before, when he was first unfaithful to his wife. He could not repent that he, a handsome, amorous man of thirty-four, was not in love with his wife, the mother of five living and two dead children, who was only a year younger than he. He repented only that he had not known how to hide it better from his wife. But he felt the whole weight of his position, and he pitied his wife, the children and himself. Perhaps he would have managed to hide his sins from his wife better if he had expected the news to affect her so. He had never thought the question out clearly, but he had a vague notion that his wife had long suspected him of being unfaithful and was shutting her eyes to it. It even seemed to him that she, a worn-out, ageing woman, no longer pretty and in no way remarkable, simple, merely a kind mother of a family, ought out of a sense of fairness to be indulgent. It turned out to be quite the opposite.

“Oh, it’s terrible! Oh dear, oh dear! Terrible!” Stepan Arkadyich kept repeating to himself, and could think of nothing. “And how good it all was until this, how well we lived! She was contented, happy with the children; I never stood in her way in anything; I let her fuss over the children and the house as she liked. True, it isn’t nice that she was a governess in our own house. It isn’t nice! There is something trivial, something vulgar, in making up to one’s own governess. But what a governess!” (He vividly remembered Mlle Roland’s mischievous black eyes and her smile.) “But after all, while she was in our house I allowed myself nothing. And the worst of it is that she is already… It all has to happen as if on purpose! Oh dear, oh dear! But what, what is to be done?”

There was no answer, except that general answer which life gives to all the most complicated and insoluble questions. That answer is: one must live for the needs of the day, that is, forget oneself. To forget oneself in sleep was no longer possible, at least not until night; it was no longer possible to go back to the music the decanter-women had been singing; so one must forget oneself in the sleep of life.

“We shall see,” Stepan Arkadyich said to himself, and, getting up, he put on his grey dressing-gown with its pale blue silk lining, tied the tassels in a knot, drew a good deep breath into the broad cage of his chest, and with his usual brisk step, on his turned-out feet that carried his full body so lightly, went to the window, raised the blind and rang loudly. At the ring there came in at once his old friend, the valet Matvei, carrying his clothes, his boots and a telegram. After Matvei came the barber too, with his shaving things.
“Are there papers from the office?” asked Stepan Arkadyich, taking the telegram and sitting down at the mirror.
“On the table,” answered Matvei; he glanced at his master questioningly, with sympathy, and, after waiting a little, added with a sly smile: “They came from the carriage-hirer.”

Stepan Arkadyich said nothing and only looked at Matvei in the mirror; in the look with which their eyes met in the mirror it could be seen how well they understood each other. Stepan Arkadyich’s look seemed to ask: “Why do you tell me that? Don’t you know?”
Matvei put his hands in the pockets of his jacket, set one foot aside and looked at his master in silence, good-naturedly, smiling just a little.
“I told him to come next Sunday, and until then not to trouble you or himself for nothing,” he said, in a phrase he had evidently prepared.

Stepan Arkadyich understood that Matvei wanted to make a joke and draw attention to himself. Tearing open the telegram, he read it, guessing at the words, which were garbled as always, and his face lit up.
“Matvei, my sister Anna Arkadyevna will be here tomorrow,” he said, stopping for a moment the barber’s glossy, plump little hand, which was clearing a pink road between his long curly side-whiskers.

“Thank God,” said Matvei, showing by this answer that he understood the meaning of this visit just as well as his master did, that is, that Anna Arkadyevna, Stepan Arkadyich’s favourite sister, might help to bring husband and wife together again.
“Alone, or with her husband?” asked Matvei.
Stepan Arkadyich could not speak, since the barber was busy with his upper lip, and he raised one finger. Matvei nodded in the mirror.
“Alone. Shall I get the rooms upstairs ready?”
“Tell Darya Alexandrovna, and do as she says.”
“Darya Alexandrovna?” Matvei repeated, as though in doubt.
“Yes, tell her. And here, take the telegram, give it to her, and then tell me what she says.”
“You want to try it out,” Matvei understood; but all he said was:
“Very good, sir.”

Stepan Arkadyich was already washed and combed and was getting ready to dress when Matvei, stepping slowly in his creaking boots over the soft carpet, came back into the room with the telegram in his hand. The barber had gone.

“Darya Alexandrovna told me to say that she is going away. Let him do as he pleases, that is, as you please,” he said, laughing only with his eyes; and, putting his hands in his pockets and tilting his head to one side, he fixed his eyes on his master.
Stepan Arkadyich was silent for a while. Then a kind and somewhat pitiful smile appeared on his handsome face.
“Eh? Matvei?” he said, shaking his head.
“Never mind, sir, it will all shape itself,” said Matvei.
“Shape itself?”
“Just so, sir.”
“You think so? Who is that there?” asked Stepan Arkadyich, hearing the rustle of a woman’s dress outside the door.
“It’s me, sir,” said a firm and pleasant woman’s voice, and from behind the door appeared the stern, pock-marked face of Matryona Filimonovna, the nurse.
“Well, what is it, Matryosha?” asked Stepan Arkadyich, going out to her at the door.
Although Stepan Arkadyich was entirely in the wrong towards his wife and felt it himself, almost everyone in the house, even the nurse, Darya Alexandrovna’s chief friend, was on his side.
“Well, what is it?” he said dejectedly.

“You go to her, sir, and beg her pardon once more. God willing, it will come right. She is suffering terribly, it’s a pity to look at her, and the whole house has gone topsy-turvy. You must have pity on the children, sir. Beg her pardon, sir. What else is there to do! If you like sledging, you must like pulling the sledge…”
“But she won’t see me…”
“You do your part. God is merciful; pray to God, sir, pray to God.”
“Well, all right, off you go,” said Stepan Arkadyich, suddenly blushing. “Well, let us get dressed,” he said, turning to Matvei, and threw off his dressing-gown decisively.
Matvei was already holding the shirt ready, gathered up like a horse’s collar, blowing away something invisible from it, and with evident pleasure he clothed his master’s well-tended body in it.
## Chapter III

When he was dressed, Stepan Arkadyich sprinkled himself with scent, pulled down the cuffs of his shirt, with a practised movement distributed among his pockets his cigarettes, his pocket-book, his matches, and his watch with its double chain and seals, and, shaking out his handkerchief, feeling himself clean, fragrant, healthy and physically cheerful in spite of his misfortune, he walked out, with a slight spring at each step, into the dining-room, where his coffee was already waiting for him, and beside the coffee his letters and the papers from the office.

Stepan Arkadyich sat down and read his letters. One was very unpleasant: it was from a merchant who was buying a forest on his wife’s estate. The forest had to be sold; but now, until he was reconciled with his wife, there could be no question of that. What was most unpleasant here was that a money interest was being mixed into the coming business of his reconciliation with his wife. And the thought that he might be guided by this interest, that he might seek reconciliation with his wife in order to sell this forest, that thought offended him.

When he had finished the letters, Stepan Arkadyich drew the office papers towards him, quickly leafed through two files, made a few notes with a big pencil, and, pushing the files aside, turned to his coffee; over his coffee he unfolded the morning paper, still damp, and began to read it.

Stepan Arkadyich took and read a liberal newspaper, not an extreme one, but of the tendency held by the majority. And although neither science nor art nor politics really interested him, he held firmly to the views on all these subjects held by the majority and by his paper, and changed them only when the majority changed them; or, to put it better, he did not change them, but they changed in him of themselves, without his noticing.

Stepan Arkadyich did not choose his tendency or his views; these tendencies and views came to him of themselves, exactly as he did not choose the shape of his hat or his frock-coat but took those that were being worn. And for him, living in a certain society, with the need for some activity of thought that usually develops in the years of maturity, having views was just as necessary as having a hat. If there was any reason why he preferred the liberal tendency to the conservative one, which many people of his circle also held, it was not that he found the liberal tendency more reasonable, but that it came closer to his way of life. The liberal party said that everything in Russia was bad; and indeed Stepan Arkadyich had a great many debts and decidedly too little money. The liberal party said that marriage was an outworn institution and must be rebuilt; and indeed family life gave Stepan Arkadyich little pleasure and forced him to lie and pretend, which was so contrary to his nature. The liberal party said, or rather implied, that religion was only a bridle for the barbarous part of the population; and indeed Stepan Arkadyich could not stand through even a short church service without pain in his legs, and could not understand what all those dreadful and high-flown words about the other world were for, when life in this one could be very jolly. At the same time Stepan Arkadyich, who loved a merry joke, liked now and then to puzzle some meek person by saying that if one was going to be proud of one’s ancestry, one ought not to stop at Rurik and disown the first founder of the line, the ape. And so the liberal tendency became a habit with Stepan Arkadyich, and he loved his newspaper, as he loved a cigar after dinner, for the light mist it produced in his head. He read the leading article, which explained that in our time it was quite pointless to raise an outcry that radicalism threatened to swallow up all the conservative elements and that the government was obliged to take measures to crush the hydra of revolution; that, on the contrary, “in our opinion the danger lies not in an imaginary hydra of revolution, but in the obstinacy of traditionalism, which holds back progress,” and so on. He read another article too, a financial one, in which Bentham and Mill were mentioned and fine little pins were stuck into the ministry. With the quickness of mind that was his, he understood the point of every pin: from whom and at whom and on what occasion it was aimed; and that, as always, gave him a certain pleasure. But today the pleasure was poisoned by the memory of Matryona Filimonovna’s advice and of how badly things stood in the house. He read, too, that Count Beust was said to have travelled to Wiesbaden, and that there need be no more grey hair, and of the sale of a light carriage, and an offer from a young person; but this news did not give him, as it used to, a quiet ironic pleasure.

When he had finished the paper, a second cup of coffee and a white roll with butter, he got up, shook the crumbs of the roll off his waistcoat and, squaring his broad chest, smiled joyfully, not because there was anything especially pleasant in his heart: the joyful smile came from a good digestion.
But this joyful smile at once reminded him of everything, and he grew thoughtful.
Two children’s voices (Stepan Arkadyich recognized the voices of Grisha, the younger boy, and Tanya, the elder girl) were heard outside the door. They were pulling something along and had dropped it.
“I told you you can’t put passengers on the roof,” the girl was shouting in English. “Now pick them up!”
“Everything is in confusion,” thought Stepan Arkadyich. “There are the children running about on their own.” And, going to the door, he called them.
They dropped the box that stood for a train and came in to their father.

The girl, her father’s favourite, ran in boldly, hugged him and, laughing, hung on his neck, delighting as always in the familiar smell of scent that came from his whiskers. Kissing him at last on his face, which was flushed from stooping and shining with tenderness, the girl unclasped her hands and wanted to run back; but her father held her.
“How is mama?” said her father, stroking his daughter’s smooth, soft little neck. “Good morning,” he said, smiling at the boy, who was greeting him.
He knew that he loved the boy less, and he always tried to be even-handed; but the boy felt it, and did not answer his father’s cold smile with a smile.
“Mama? She’s up,” answered the girl.
Stepan Arkadyich sighed. “That means she didn’t sleep all night again,” he thought.
“Well, is she cheerful?”

The girl knew that there had been a quarrel between her father and mother, and that her mother could not be cheerful, and that her father must know it, and that he was pretending when he asked about it so lightly. And she blushed for her father. He understood this at once and blushed too.
“I don’t know,” she said. “She didn’t tell us to do lessons; she told us to go for a walk with Miss Hull to grandmama’s.”
“Well, run along, my little Tanchurochka. Oh yes, wait a moment,” he said, still holding her and stroking her tender little hand.
He took down from the mantelpiece, where he had put it the day before, a little box of sweets, and gave her two, picking out her favourites, a chocolate one and a fondant.
“For Grisha?” said the girl, pointing to the chocolate one.
“Yes, yes.” And, stroking her little shoulder once more, he kissed her at the roots of her hair and on the neck, and let her go.
“The carriage is ready,” said Matvei. “And there is a woman with a petition,” he added.
“Has she been here long?” asked Stepan Arkadyich.
“Half an hour or so.”
“How many times have I told you to let me know at once!”
“You must be let have your coffee in peace at least,” said Matvei, in that friendly, gruff tone with which it was impossible to be angry.
“Well, show her in quickly,” said Oblonsky, frowning with vexation.

The petitioner, a Captain Kalinin’s wife, was asking for something impossible and senseless; but Stepan Arkadyich, as was his custom, sat her down, listened to her attentively without interrupting, and gave her detailed advice on whom to apply to and how, and even, briskly and fluently, in his large, sprawling, handsome and clear hand, wrote her a little note to a person who might help her. Having sent the captain’s wife away, Stepan Arkadyich took his hat and stopped, trying to remember whether he had forgotten anything. It turned out that he had forgotten nothing except what he wanted to forget: his wife.

“Ah yes!” He lowered his head, and his handsome face took on a melancholy expression. “To go, or not to go?” he said to himself. And an inner voice told him that he ought not to go, that nothing could come of it but falseness; that it was impossible to set their relations right, to mend them, because it was impossible to make her attractive again and capable of arousing love, or to make him an old man incapable of loving. Nothing but falseness and lies could come of it now; and falseness and lies were against his nature.

“But some time it has to be done; it can’t stay like this, after all,” he said, trying to give himself courage. He straightened his chest, took out a cigarette, lit it, drew on it twice, threw it into the mother-of-pearl shell that served as an ashtray, crossed the gloomy drawing-room with quick steps, and opened the other door, into his wife’s bedroom.
## Chapter IV

Darya Alexandrovna, in a loose jacket, with the plaits of her once thick and beautiful hair, now thin, pinned up at the back of her head, with a sunken, thin face and large frightened eyes that stood out because her face was so thin, was standing among things scattered about the room, in front of an open chiffonier, from which she was taking something out. Hearing her husband’s steps, she stopped, looking at the door and trying in vain to give her face a stern and contemptuous expression. She felt that she was afraid of him and afraid of the coming interview. She had just been trying to do what she had tried to do ten times already in these three days: to sort out her own and the children’s things, which she would take to her mother’s, and again she could not bring herself to it; but now too, as on the earlier occasions, she told herself that things could not stay like this, that she must do something, punish him, shame him, revenge herself on him for at least a small part of the pain he had caused her. She still said that she would leave him, but she felt that it was impossible; it was impossible because she could not break the habit of regarding him as her husband and of loving him. Besides, she felt that if here, in her own house, she could hardly manage to look after her five children, they would be still worse off wherever she went with them all. As it was, in these three days the youngest had fallen ill because he had been given bad broth, and the others had gone almost without dinner the day before. She felt that it was impossible to leave; but, deceiving herself, she went on sorting things and pretending she would go.

Seeing her husband, she lowered her hands into the drawer of the chiffonier as though looking for something, and looked round at him only when he had come right up to her. But her face, to which she had wanted to give a stern and resolute expression, expressed bewilderment and suffering.
“Dolly!” he said in a low, timid voice. He drew his head down into his shoulders and wanted to look pitiful and submissive, but all the same he was radiant with freshness and health.

With a quick glance she looked over his figure, radiant with freshness and health, from head to foot. “Yes, he is happy and contented!” she thought. “And I?… And that disgusting good nature, for which everyone loves him and praises him so; I hate that good nature of his,” she thought. Her mouth tightened; a muscle of her cheek began to twitch on the right side of her pale, nervous face.
“What do you want?” she said in a quick, deep voice that was not her own.
“Dolly!” he repeated, with a tremor in his voice. “Anna is coming today.”
“Well, what is that to me? I cannot receive her!” she cried.
“But you must, after all, Dolly…”
“Go away, go away, go away!” she cried without looking at him, as though the cry were wrung from her by physical pain.

Stepan Arkadyich could be calm when he thought about his wife; he could hope that everything would shape itself, as Matvei put it, and could calmly read the paper and drink his coffee; but when he saw her tormented, suffering face and heard that tone of voice, submissive and despairing, his breath caught, something rose in his throat, and his eyes shone with tears.
“My God, what have I done! Dolly! For God’s sake!… After all…” He could not go on; a sob caught in his throat.
She slammed the chiffonier shut and looked at him.
“Dolly, what can I say?… Only one thing: forgive, forgive… Remember, can’t nine years of life make up for a minute, a minute…”
She stood with her eyes lowered and listened, waiting for what he would say, as though begging him to persuade her somehow that it was not so.

“A minute… a minute of being carried away…” he brought out, and wanted to go on; but at that word her lips tightened again, as if from physical pain, and again the muscle of her cheek began to jump on the right side of her face.
“Go away, get out of here!” she shouted still more shrilly. “And don’t talk to me about your infatuations, about your vileness!”
She wanted to leave, but she swayed and took hold of the back of a chair to steady herself. His face broadened, his lips swelled, his eyes filled with tears.

“Dolly!” he said, now sobbing. “For God’s sake, think of the children; they are not to blame. I am to blame; punish me, tell me how to atone for my guilt. Whatever I can do, I am ready for anything! I am to blame; there are no words to say how much I am to blame! But, Dolly, forgive me!”
She sat down. He heard her heavy, loud breathing, and he felt inexpressibly sorry for her. Several times she wanted to begin speaking, but could not. He waited.

“You remember the children when you want to play with them, but I remember them and know that they are ruined now,” she said: evidently one of the phrases she had repeated to herself more than once in these three days.
She had said “thou” to him, and he looked at her gratefully and moved to take her hand, but she drew away from him with disgust.

“I remember the children, and for that reason I would do anything in the world to save them; but I don’t know myself how I am to save them: by taking them away from their father, or by leaving them with a depraved father, yes, a depraved father… Well, tell me, after what… has happened, is it possible for us to live together? Is it possible? Tell me, is it possible?” she repeated, raising her voice. “After my husband, the father of my children, starts a love affair with his own children’s governess…”
“But what… what is to be done?” he said in a pitiful voice, not knowing himself what he was saying, and lowering his head more and more.

“You are vile to me, disgusting!” she shouted, growing more and more heated. “Your tears are water! You never loved me; there is neither heart nor honour in you! You are loathsome to me, disgusting, a stranger, yes, a stranger!” With pain and fury she pronounced that word, so terrible to her: stranger.

He looked at her, and the fury that showed in her face frightened and astonished him. He did not understand that his pity for her was what exasperated her. She saw in him regret for her, but not love. “No, she hates me. She will not forgive,” he thought.
“This is terrible! Terrible!” he said.
At that moment a child cried in the next room, probably after a fall; Darya Alexandrovna listened, and her face suddenly softened.
For a few seconds she was evidently coming to herself, as though not knowing where she was or what she had to do; then, getting up quickly, she moved towards the door.
“She does love my child, after all,” he thought, noticing the change in her face at the child’s cry, “my child; so how can she hate me?”
“Dolly, one word more,” he said, following her.
“If you follow me, I shall call the servants, the children! Let everyone know that you are a scoundrel! I am leaving today, and you can live here with your mistress!”
And she went out, slamming the door.

Stepan Arkadyich sighed, wiped his face and walked out of the room with quiet steps. “Matvei says it will shape itself; but how? I can’t even see the possibility. Oh, oh, how horrible! And how trivially she shouted,” he said to himself, remembering her shout and the words “scoundrel” and “mistress”. “And perhaps the maids heard! Horribly trivial, horribly.” Stepan Arkadyich stood alone for a few seconds, wiped his eyes, sighed, and, straightening his chest, went out of the room.

It was Friday, and in the dining-room the German clockmaker was winding the clocks. Stepan Arkadyich remembered his joke about this punctual, bald clockmaker, that the German “had been wound up for life himself, in order to wind clocks”, and he smiled. Stepan Arkadyich loved a good joke. “And perhaps it will shape itself! A good little word, that: shape itself,” he thought. “I must tell that one.”
“Matvei!” he called. “So arrange everything with Marya in the sitting-room for Anna Arkadyevna,” he said to Matvei when he appeared.
“Very good, sir.”
Stepan Arkadyich put on his fur coat and went out onto the porch.
“Will you not be dining at home?” said Matvei, seeing him off.
“That depends. Here, take this for the housekeeping,” he said, handing him ten roubles from his pocket-book. “Will that be enough?”
“Enough or not enough, we shall have to manage, it seems,” said Matvei, slamming the carriage door and stepping back onto the porch.

Meanwhile Darya Alexandrovna, having calmed the child and understood from the sound of the carriage that he had gone, went back to the bedroom. It was her only refuge from the household cares that crowded round her as soon as she went out. Even now, in the short time she had been in the nursery, the English governess and Matryona Filimonovna had managed to put several questions to her that would not wait and that she alone could answer: what were the children to wear for their walk? Should they be given milk? Should not someone be sent for another cook?

“Oh, leave me alone, leave me alone!” she said, and, going back to the bedroom, sat down again in the same place where she had talked with her husband, clasping her thin hands, with the rings slipping down off her bony fingers, and began going over the whole conversation in her memory. “He has gone! But how has he ended it with her?” she thought. “Can it be that he sees her? Why didn’t I ask him? No, no, we cannot come together again. Even if we stay in the same house, we are strangers. Strangers for ever!” she repeated again, with a special meaning, that word so terrible to her. “And how I loved him, my God, how I loved him!… How I loved him! And even now, don’t I love him? Don’t I love him more than before? The terrible thing, above all, is that…” she began, but did not finish her thought, because Matryona Filimonovna put her head in at the door.
“Do let us send for my brother,” she said. “He can get the dinner ready at least; otherwise, like yesterday, the children won’t have eaten till six o’clock.”
“Well, all right, I will come out in a minute and see to it. And has someone been sent for fresh milk?”
And Darya Alexandrovna plunged into the cares of the day and for a time drowned her grief in them.
## Chapter V

Stepan Arkadyich had done well at school thanks to his good abilities, but he had been lazy and mischievous, and so had come out near the bottom; yet in spite of his always dissipated life, his modest rank and his not very advanced years, he held the honourable and well-paid post of head of one of the government offices in Moscow. He had obtained this post through his sister Anna’s husband, Alexei Alexandrovich Karenin, who held one of the most important positions in the ministry to which the office belonged; but if Karenin had not appointed his brother-in-law to this post, then through a hundred other people, brothers, sisters, relations, cousins, uncles, aunts, Stiva Oblonsky would have obtained this post or another like it, with a salary of some six thousand, which he needed, since his affairs, in spite of his wife’s considerable fortune, were in disorder.

Half of Moscow and Petersburg were Stepan Arkadyich’s relations and friends. He was born among the people who were, and who became, the powerful of this world. A third of the statesmen, the old ones, had been friends of his father and had known him in his little shirt; another third were on “thou” terms with him; and the last third were good acquaintances. Consequently the distributors of earthly blessings, in the form of posts, leases, concessions and the like, were all his friends and could not pass over one of their own; and Oblonsky did not need to try particularly hard to get a profitable post; he needed only not to refuse, not to envy, not to quarrel, not to take offence, which, from the good nature that was his, he never did. It would have seemed ridiculous to him if he had been told that he would not get a post with the salary he needed, all the more since he did not ask for anything extraordinary; he wanted only what men of his own age were getting, and he could carry out an office of that kind no worse than anyone else.

Stepan Arkadyich was liked by everyone who knew him, not only for his kind, cheerful temper and unquestionable honesty; there was something in him, in his handsome, bright appearance, his shining eyes, black brows and hair, the whiteness and rosiness of his face, that acted physically, in a friendly and cheerful way, on the people who met him. “Aha! Stiva! Oblonsky! Here he is!” people said almost always, with a joyful smile, when they met him. And if it sometimes happened that after a conversation with him it turned out that nothing particularly joyful had happened, the next day, or the day after, everyone was just as glad again to meet him.

Now in his third year as head of one of the government offices in Moscow, Stepan Arkadyich had won, besides affection, the respect of his colleagues, his subordinates, his superiors and everyone who had dealings with him. The chief qualities that earned Stepan Arkadyich this general respect in the service were: first, his extraordinary indulgence towards people, founded in him on the awareness of his own failings; second, his complete liberalism, not the kind he read about in the newspapers but the kind that was in his blood, by which he treated all people perfectly equally and alike, whatever their fortune or rank; and third, and most important, his complete indifference to the business he was engaged in, as a result of which he never got carried away and never made mistakes.

Arriving at his place of work, Stepan Arkadyich, accompanied by the respectful porter, walked with his portfolio into his little private room, put on his uniform and went into the office. The clerks and officials all stood up, bowing cheerfully and respectfully. Stepan Arkadyich hurried, as always, to his place, shook hands with the members of the board and sat down. He joked and chatted exactly as much as was proper, and began the business of the day. No one knew better than Stepan Arkadyich how to find that boundary of freedom, simplicity and formality that is needed to make business pleasant. The secretary, cheerfully and respectfully, like everyone in Stepan Arkadyich’s office, came up with the papers and said, in that familiar and liberal tone which Stepan Arkadyich had introduced:
“We have managed to get the information from the Penza provincial board after all. Here it is, if you please…”
“Got it at last?” said Stepan Arkadyich, marking the paper with his finger. “Well, gentlemen…” And the session began.

“If only they knew,” he thought, bending his head with a look of importance as he listened to the report, “what a guilty little boy their president was half an hour ago!” And his eyes laughed while the report was read. Business was to go on without a break until two o’clock, and at two there would be an interval and lunch.

It was not yet two when the large glass doors of the office suddenly opened and someone came in. All the members, from under the portrait and from behind the emblem of justice, glad of a distraction, looked round at the door; but the attendant standing by the door at once drove the newcomer out and closed the glass door behind him.

When the case had been read through, Stepan Arkadyich got up and stretched, and, paying his tribute to the liberalism of the times, took out a cigarette right there in the office and went into his private room. Two of his colleagues, the old official Nikitin and the gentleman of the bedchamber Grinevich, went out with him.
“We shall have time to finish after lunch,” said Stepan Arkadyich.
“Plenty of time!” said Nikitin.
“He must be a fine rogue, that Fomin,” said Grinevich of one of the persons involved in the case they were examining.
Stepan Arkadyich frowned at Grinevich’s words, letting it be felt by this that it was improper to form a judgement too soon, and gave him no answer.
“Who was that who came in?” he asked the attendant.
“Some man, your excellency, pushed his way in without asking, the moment I turned my back. He was asking for you. I told him: when the members come out, then…”
“Where is he?”

“He’s gone out into the hall, I expect; he was walking about here all the time. That’s him,” said the attendant, pointing to a strongly built, broad-shouldered man with a curly beard who, without taking off his sheepskin cap, was running quickly and lightly up the worn steps of the stone staircase. One of the officials coming down, a thin man with a portfolio, stopped and looked disapprovingly at the legs of the man running up, and then glanced questioningly at Oblonsky.
Stepan Arkadyich was standing at the top of the stairs. His good-naturedly beaming face above the embroidered collar of his uniform beamed still more when he recognized the man running up.

“So it is! Levin, at last!” he said with a friendly, mocking smile, looking at Levin as he came up. “How is it you didn’t scorn to look for me in this den?” said Stepan Arkadyich, and, not content with a handshake, he kissed his friend. “Have you been here long?”
“I have only just arrived, and I wanted very much to see you,” answered Levin, looking round shyly and at the same time angrily and uneasily.
“Well, let’s go into my room,” said Stepan Arkadyich, who knew his friend’s proud and resentful shyness; and, seizing him by the arm, he drew him along after him, as though steering him past dangers.

Stepan Arkadyich was on “thou” terms with almost all his acquaintances: with old men of sixty, with boys of twenty, with actors, with ministers, with merchants and with adjutant-generals, so that a great many of those who were on “thou” terms with him stood at the two extreme ends of the social ladder and would have been very much surprised to learn that through Oblonsky they had something in common. He was on “thou” terms with everyone he drank champagne with, and he drank champagne with everyone; and so, when in the presence of his subordinates he met any of his shameful “thous”, as he jokingly called many of his friends, he knew, with the tact that was his, how to lessen the unpleasantness of the impression for his subordinates. Levin was not a shameful “thou”, but Oblonsky with his tact felt that Levin thought he might not wish to show his intimacy with him in front of his subordinates, and so he hurried to take him into his room.

Levin was almost the same age as Oblonsky, and was on “thou” terms with him not through champagne alone. Levin had been his comrade and friend in early youth. They loved each other in spite of the difference in their characters and tastes, as friends love each other who have come together in early youth. But in spite of that, as often happens between people who have chosen different kinds of work, each of them, though in argument he justified the other’s work, in his heart despised it. To each it seemed that the life his friend was leading was only a phantom. Oblonsky could not keep back a slight mocking smile at the sight of Levin. How many times he had seen him come to Moscow from the country, where he was doing something, though what exactly Stepan Arkadyich could never properly understand, nor was he interested; Levin always came to Moscow excited, hurried, a little ill at ease and irritated by his own unease, and usually with a completely new, unexpected view of things. Stepan Arkadyich laughed at this and loved it. In just the same way Levin in his heart despised his friend’s town way of life and his service, which he considered nonsense, and laughed at them. But the difference was that Oblonsky, doing what everyone does, laughed self-confidently and good-naturedly, while Levin laughed without self-confidence, and sometimes angrily.

“We have been expecting you for a long time,” said Stepan Arkadyich, going into his room and letting go of Levin’s arm, as if to show that here the dangers were over. “I am very, very glad to see you,” he went on. “Well, how are you? What’s new? When did you arrive?”

Levin was silent, looking at the unfamiliar faces of Oblonsky’s two colleagues, and in particular at the hand of the elegant Grinevich, with such white slender fingers, such long yellow nails curving at the ends, and such enormous shining cuff-links on his shirt, that these hands evidently absorbed all his attention and left him no freedom of thought. Oblonsky noticed this at once and smiled.

“Ah yes, allow me to introduce you,” he said. “My colleagues: Filipp Ivanych Nikitin, Mikhail Stanislavich Grinevich,” and, turning to Levin: “A zemstvo man, a new zemstvo man, a gymnast who lifts two hundred pounds with one hand, a cattle-breeder and a hunter, and my friend, Konstantin Dmitrich Levin, the brother of Sergei Ivanych Koznyshev.”
“Delighted,” said the little old man.
“I have the honour of knowing your brother, Sergei Ivanych,” said Grinevich, holding out his slender hand with its long nails.

Levin frowned, shook the hand coldly and at once turned to Oblonsky. Although he had a great respect for his half-brother, the writer, known to all Russia, he could not bear it when people addressed him not as Konstantin Levin but as the brother of the famous Koznyshev.
“No, I am not a zemstvo man any more. I have quarrelled with everyone and don’t go to the meetings any more,” he said, turning to Oblonsky.
“That was quick!” said Oblonsky with a smile. “But how? Why?”

“It’s a long story. I’ll tell you some time,” said Levin, but at once began telling it. “Well, to put it briefly, I became convinced that there is no zemstvo activity and cannot be any,” he began, as though someone had just insulted him. “On one side it’s a toy, they play at parliament, and I am neither young enough nor old enough to amuse myself with toys; and on the other side” (he stammered) “it is a means for the district coterie to make a little money. Before, it was the wardships and the courts, and now it’s the zemstvo… not in the form of bribes, but in the form of unearned salaries,” he said, as hotly as if someone present had been disputing his opinion.
“Aha! I see you are in a new phase again, a conservative one,” said Stepan Arkadyich. “But we’ll talk of that later.”
“Yes, later. But I needed to see you,” said Levin, staring with hatred at Grinevich’s hand.
Stepan Arkadyich smiled almost imperceptibly.
“How is it you said you would never again wear European clothes?” he said, looking over his new suit, evidently from a French tailor. “Just so! I see: a new phase.”

Levin suddenly blushed, but not as grown men blush, slightly, without noticing it themselves, but as boys blush, feeling that they are ridiculous in their shyness, and as a result ashamed and blushing still more, almost to tears. And it was so strange to see this intelligent, manly face in such a childish state that Oblonsky stopped looking at him.
“Well, where shall we meet? I very, very much need to talk to you,” said Levin.
Oblonsky seemed to think.
“I’ll tell you what: let’s go to Gurin’s for lunch and talk there. I am free till three.”
“No,” answered Levin, after thinking, “I still have to go somewhere else.”
“Well, all right, then let’s dine together.”
“Dine? But there’s nothing special, you know, only a couple of words to say, a question to ask, and we can have a talk afterwards.”
“Then say your couple of words now, and we’ll have the talk over dinner.”
“The couple of words are these,” said Levin; “though it’s nothing special.”
His face suddenly took on an angry expression, which came from the effort to overcome his shyness.
“What are the Shcherbatskys doing? Is everything as it was?” he said.
Stepan Arkadyich, who had long known that Levin was in love with his sister-in-law Kitty, smiled almost imperceptibly, and his eyes shone merrily.
“You said a couple of words, but I can’t answer in a couple of words, because… Excuse me for a minute…”

The secretary came in, with familiar respectfulness and with that modest awareness, common to all secretaries, of his superiority over his chief in knowledge of the business; he came up to Oblonsky with some papers and began, under the guise of a question, to explain some difficulty. Stepan Arkadyich, without hearing him out, laid his hand kindly on the secretary’s sleeve.

“No, you just do it the way I said,” he said, softening the remark with a smile; and, explaining briefly how he understood the matter, he pushed the papers away and said: “Do it that way, please. Please, that way, Zakhar Nikitich.”

The embarrassed secretary withdrew. Levin, who during the consultation with the secretary had quite recovered from his embarrassment, was standing with both elbows leaning on a chair, and on his face was a look of mocking attention.
“I don’t understand it, I don’t understand it,” he said.
“What don’t you understand?” said Oblonsky, smiling just as cheerfully and taking out a cigarette. He was expecting some odd sally from Levin.
“I don’t understand what you are doing,” said Levin, shrugging his shoulders. “How can you do this seriously?”
“Why not?”
“Why, because there is nothing to do.”
“You think so, but we are snowed under with work.”
“Paper work. Well, yes, you have a gift for that,” added Levin.
“You mean you think I am lacking in something?”

“Perhaps I do,” said Levin. “But all the same I admire your grandeur and am proud that my friend is such a great man. But you haven’t answered my question,” he added, with a desperate effort looking Oblonsky straight in the eyes.

“Well, all right, all right. Wait a little, and you will come to this too. It’s all very well while you have three thousand desyatinas in the Karazinsky district, and such muscles, and the freshness of a girl of twelve; but you will come over to us too. Yes, as for what you asked: there is no change, but it’s a pity you have stayed away so long.”
“Why?” asked Levin in alarm.
“Oh, nothing,” answered Oblonsky. “We’ll talk. But what, exactly, have you come for?”
“Oh, we’ll talk about that later too,” said Levin, blushing again to his ears.

“Well, all right. I understand,” said Stepan Arkadyich. “You see, I would ask you to my house, but my wife is not quite well. But here’s an idea: if you want to see them, they are sure to be at the Zoological Gardens today between four and five. Kitty goes skating. You drive there, and I’ll come by, and we’ll go and dine somewhere together.”
“Splendid. Well, goodbye.”
“Mind now, I know you, you’ll forget, or suddenly go off to the country!” Stepan Arkadyich called out, laughing.
“No, I shan’t.”
And, remembering that he had forgotten to take leave of Oblonsky’s colleagues only when he was already in the doorway, Levin went out of the room.
“That must be a very energetic gentleman,” said Grinevich when Levin had gone.

“Yes, my dear fellow,” said Stepan Arkadyich, shaking his head, “there’s a lucky man! Three thousand desyatinas in the Karazinsky district, everything ahead of him, and so much freshness! Not like the rest of us.”
“What have you to complain of, Stepan Arkadyich?”
“Oh, it’s bad, things are poor,” said Stepan Arkadyich, with a heavy sigh.
## Part One · Chapter VI

When Oblonsky asked Levin what, exactly, he had come for, Levin blushed and was angry with himself for blushing, because he could not answer him: “I have come to propose to your sister-in-law,” though that was the only thing he had come for.

The Levins and the Shcherbatskys were old Moscow noble families and had always been on close and friendly terms. The tie had grown still stronger during Levin’s student days. He had prepared for the university together with the young Prince Shcherbatsky, the brother of Dolly and Kitty, and had entered it together with him. At that time Levin was often at the Shcherbatskys’ house, and he fell in love with the Shcherbatskys’ house. Strange as it may seem, Konstantin Levin was in love precisely with the house, with the family, and especially with the women of the Shcherbatsky family. Levin himself did not remember his mother, and his only sister was older than he, so that in the Shcherbatskys’ house he saw for the first time that very world of an old, educated and honourable noble family of which he had been deprived by the death of his father and mother. All the members of this family, especially the women, seemed to him to be wrapped in a kind of mysterious, poetic veil, and not only did he see no faults in them, but under that poetic veil that covered them he supposed the loftiest feelings and every possible perfection. Why these three young ladies had to speak French and English on alternate days; why at certain hours they took turns playing the piano, whose sounds could always be heard upstairs in the brother’s room, where the students worked; why these teachers of French literature, of music, of drawing, of dancing kept coming; why at certain hours all three young ladies, with Mlle Linon, drove up in the carriage to the Tverskoy Boulevard in their satin fur coats, Dolly in a long one, Natalie in a half-length one, and Kitty in a quite short one, so that her shapely little legs in tightly drawn red stockings were in full view; why they had to walk along the Tverskoy Boulevard accompanied by a footman with a gold cockade on his hat: all this, and much else that went on in their mysterious world, he did not understand; but he knew that everything that went on there was beautiful, and he was in love precisely with the mystery of what went on.

During his student days he had very nearly fallen in love with the eldest, Dolly, but she was soon married to Oblonsky. Then he began to fall in love with the second. He seemed to feel that he had to fall in love with one of the sisters; only he could not make out which one. But Natalie too, as soon as she came out into society, married the diplomat Lvov. Kitty was still a child when Levin left the university. Young Shcherbatsky joined the navy and was drowned in the Baltic, and Levin’s relations with the Shcherbatskys, in spite of his friendship with Oblonsky, became rarer. But when this year, at the beginning of winter, Levin came to Moscow after a year in the country and saw the Shcherbatskys, he understood which of the three he had really been destined to fall in love with.

It would seem that nothing could be simpler than for him, a man of good family, rich rather than poor, thirty-two years old, to propose to the Princess Shcherbatskaya; in all likelihood he would at once have been considered a good match. But Levin was in love, and so it seemed to him that Kitty was such a perfection in every respect, a being so far above everything earthly, and he such an earthly, low being, that there could be no thought of others, or she herself, considering him worthy of her.

After spending two months in Moscow as if in a daze, seeing Kitty almost every day in society, which he began to go into so as to meet her, Levin suddenly decided that it could not be, and went away to the country.

Levin’s conviction that it could not be was founded on this: that in the eyes of her family he was an unprofitable, unworthy match for the lovely Kitty, and that Kitty herself could not love him. In her family’s eyes he had no customary, definite occupation and no position in society, whereas his comrades now, when he was thirty-two, were already one a colonel and aide-de-camp, another a professor, another the director of a bank and of railways, or the head of a government office, like Oblonsky; while he (he knew very well how he must look to others) was a landowner occupied with breeding cows, shooting snipe and putting up buildings: that is, a giftless fellow who had come to nothing, and who was doing, as society understood it, exactly what people do who are good for nothing.

And the mysterious, lovely Kitty herself could not love a man as plain as he considered himself, and above all such a simple man, in no way out of the ordinary. Besides, his former relation to Kitty, the relation of a grown man to a child, because of his friendship with her brother, seemed to him yet another barrier to love. A plain, kind man such as he considered himself could, he supposed, be loved as a friend; but to be loved with the kind of love with which he loved Kitty, one had to be handsome, and above all a special man.
He had heard that women often love plain, simple men, but he did not believe it, because he judged by himself, and he himself could love only beautiful, mysterious and special women.

But after two months alone in the country he became convinced that this was not one of those infatuations he had felt in early youth; that this feeling did not give him a moment’s peace; that he could not live without settling the question of whether she would or would not be his wife; and that his despair came only from his imagination, that he had no proof whatever that he would be refused. And so he had now come to Moscow with the firm decision to propose and to marry if he was accepted. Or… he could not think of what would become of him if he was refused.
## Chapter VII

Arriving in Moscow by the morning train, Levin put up at the house of his elder half-brother on his mother’s side, Koznyshev, and, after changing, went into his study, intending to tell him at once what he had come for and to ask his advice; but his brother was not alone. With him sat a well-known professor of philosophy who had come from Kharkov expressly to clear up a misunderstanding that had arisen between them over a very important philosophical question. The professor was carrying on a heated polemic against the materialists, and Sergei Koznyshev had followed this polemic with interest and, after reading the professor’s latest article, had written him his objections in a letter; he reproached the professor for making too great concessions to the materialists. And the professor had come at once to talk it out. The talk was about a fashionable question: is there a boundary between psychical and physiological phenomena in human activity, and where does it lie?
Sergei Ivanovich met his brother with the smile, kind and cold, that he had for everyone, and, introducing him to the professor, went on with the conversation.

The little yellow man in spectacles, with a narrow forehead, turned from the conversation for a moment to greet him, and then went on talking without paying any attention to Levin. Levin sat down to wait until the professor left, but soon became interested in the subject of the conversation.

Levin had come across the articles that were being discussed in the journals and had read them, interested in them as a development of the foundations of natural science, familiar to him as a natural scientist from the university; but he had never connected these scientific conclusions about the origin of man as an animal, about reflexes, about biology and sociology, with those questions about the meaning of life and death for himself which had lately come to his mind more and more often.

Listening to his brother’s conversation with the professor, he noticed that they connected the scientific questions with the questions of the heart; several times they almost came up to these questions; but each time, as soon as they came close to what seemed to him the most important thing, they at once hurriedly drew back and sank again into the region of fine subdivisions, reservations, quotations, allusions, references to authorities, and he could hardly understand what they were talking about.

“I cannot admit,” said Sergei Ivanovich, with the clearness and precision of expression and the elegance of diction that were usual with him, “I cannot in any case agree with Keiss that my whole idea of the external world comes from impressions. The most fundamental concept, that of being, I have not received through sensation, for there is not even a special organ for conveying that concept.”

“Yes, but they, Wurst, and Knaust, and Pripasov, will answer you that your consciousness of being comes from the sum of all the sensations, that this consciousness of being is the result of sensations. Wurst even says outright that, as soon as there is no sensation, there is no concept of being either.”
“I would say the reverse,” Sergei Ivanovich began…
But here again it seemed to Levin that, having come up to the most important thing, they were drawing back again, and he made up his mind to put a question to the professor.
“So, if my senses are destroyed, if my body dies, there can be no existence of any kind any more?” he asked.

The professor, with vexation and as if with a mental pain at being interrupted, looked round at the strange questioner, who looked more like a barge-hauler than a philosopher, and moved his eyes to Sergei Ivanovich, as though asking: what is there to say to that? But Sergei Ivanovich, who spoke with nothing like the professor’s strain and one-sidedness, and who had room enough in his head both to answer the professor and at the same time to understand the simple and natural point of view from which the question had been put, smiled and said:
“That question we have no right to decide as yet…”

“We have no data,” the professor confirmed, and went on with his arguments. “No,” he said, “I point out that if, as Pripasov says plainly, sensation does have impression as its basis, then we must strictly distinguish these two concepts.”
Levin listened no more, and waited for the professor to leave.
## Chapter VIII
When the professor had gone, Sergei Ivanovich turned to his brother.
“I am very glad you have come. For long? How is the farming?”
Levin knew that farming interested his elder brother very little and that he had asked about it only as a concession to him, and so he answered only about the sale of the wheat and about money.

Levin had meant to tell his brother of his intention to marry and to ask his advice; he had even firmly decided to. But when he saw his brother, listened to his conversation with the professor, when he heard afterwards the involuntarily patronizing tone in which his brother asked him about the affairs of the estate (their mother’s estate had not been divided, and Levin managed both shares), Levin felt that for some reason he could not begin to talk to his brother about his decision to marry. He felt that his brother would not look at it as he would have liked.
“Well, how is your zemstvo getting on?” asked Sergei Ivanovich, who was very much interested in the zemstvo and attached great importance to it.
“Oh, I really don’t know…”
“What? But you are a member of the board, aren’t you?”
“No, not a member any more; I have resigned,” answered Konstantin Levin, “and I don’t go to the meetings any more.”
“A pity!” said Sergei Ivanovich, frowning.
To justify himself, Levin began describing what went on at the meetings in his district.

“That’s how it always is!” Sergei Ivanovich interrupted him. “We Russians are always like that. Perhaps it is even a good trait of ours, this ability to see our own failings; but we overdo it, we console ourselves with irony, which is always ready on our tongues. I will tell you only this: give the same rights as our zemstvo institutions to another European people, and the Germans and the English would work them up into freedom, while we only laugh.”
“But what is to be done?” said Levin guiltily. “It was my last experiment. And I tried with all my heart. I can’t. I am not capable of it.”
“Not incapable,” said Sergei Ivanovich. “You don’t look at the thing in the right way.”
“Perhaps,” Levin answered dejectedly.
“And, you know, our brother Nikolai is here again.”

Nikolai was Konstantin Levin’s own elder brother and Sergei Ivanovich’s half-brother, a ruined man, who had squandered the greater part of his fortune, moved in the strangest and worst company, and quarrelled with his brothers.
“What are you saying?” Levin cried in horror. “How do you know?”
“Prokofy saw him in the street.”
“Here, in Moscow? Where is he? Do you know?” Levin got up from his chair, as though about to go at once.

“I am sorry I told you,” said Sergei Ivanych, shaking his head at his younger brother’s agitation. “I sent to find out where he is living, and sent him his promissory note to Trubin, which I had paid. This is what he answered me.”
And Sergei Ivanovich handed his brother a note from under the paperweight.
Levin read, in the strange handwriting so familiar to him: “I humbly beg to be left in peace. That is the one thing I demand of my dear brothers. Nikolai Levin.”
Levin read it and, without raising his head, stood before Sergei Ivanovich with the note in his hands.
In his soul a wish to forget his unhappy brother now was struggling with the awareness that this would be wrong.
“He obviously wants to insult me,” Sergei Ivanovich went on, “but he cannot insult me, and I would wish with all my soul to help him, but I know that it cannot be done.”
“Yes, yes,” Levin kept repeating. “I understand and value your attitude to him; but I shall go and see him.”

“If you want to, go; but I don’t advise it,” said Sergei Ivanovich. “That is, as far as I am concerned, I am not afraid of it; he will not set you against me; but for your own sake I advise you better not to go. He cannot be helped. However, do as you like.”
“Perhaps he can’t be helped, but I feel, especially at this moment (well, that’s another matter), I feel that I cannot be at peace.”

“Well, that I don’t understand,” said Sergei Ivanovich. “One thing I do understand,” he added: “it is a lesson in humility. I have come to look differently, and more indulgently, at what is called baseness since our brother Nikolai became what he is… You know what he did…”
“Oh, it’s terrible, terrible!” Levin kept repeating.

Having got his brother’s address from Sergei Ivanovich’s footman, Levin was about to go to him at once, but on second thoughts decided to put off his visit until the evening. First of all, in order to have peace of mind, he must settle the business for which he had come to Moscow. From his brother’s Levin drove to Oblonsky’s office and, having found out about the Shcherbatskys, drove to the place where he had been told he might find Kitty.
## Chapter IX

At four o’clock, feeling his heart beating, Levin got out of the cab at the Zoological Gardens and walked along the path to the ice-hills and the skating-rink, knowing for certain that he would find her there, because he had seen the Shcherbatskys’ carriage at the entrance.

It was a clear, frosty day. At the entrance stood rows of carriages, sledges, cabmen, gendarmes. Well-dressed people, their hats shining in the bright sun, swarmed at the gate and along the swept paths between the little Russian-style houses with their carved ridges; the old curly birches of the garden, all their branches weighed down with snow, seemed to have been decked out in new and solemn vestments.

He walked along the path to the rink and said to himself: “I must not get excited, I must calm down. What’s the matter with you? What do you want? Be quiet, you fool,” he said to his heart. And the more he tried to calm himself, the worse his breath caught. An acquaintance met him and called out to him, but Levin did not even recognize who it was. He came to the ice-hills, where the chains of the sledges being let down and pulled up clanked, where the sledges rolling down rumbled and merry voices rang. He went on a few steps more, and the rink opened before him, and at once, among all the skaters, he knew her.

He knew she was there by the joy and the fear that seized his heart. She was standing at the far end of the rink, talking to a lady. There seemed to be nothing special either in her dress or in her pose; but for Levin it was as easy to know her in that crowd as a rose among nettles. Everything was lit up by her. She was the smile that brightened everything round her. “Can I really go down there, onto the ice, and go up to her?” he thought. The place where she stood seemed to him an unapproachable sanctuary, and there was a moment when he almost went away, so frightened did he become. He had to make an effort over himself and reason that all sorts of people were moving around her, and that he himself might come there to skate. He went down, avoiding looking at her for long, as one avoids the sun; but, like the sun, he saw her without looking.

On that day of the week and at that time of day, people of one circle gathered on the ice, all of them acquainted with one another. There were masters of skating there, showing off their art, and learners pushing chairs in front of them, with timid, awkward movements, and boys, and old people skating for their health; all of them seemed to Levin chosen, lucky people, because they were here, near her. All the skaters, it seemed, with perfect indifference overtook her, caught up with her, even talked to her, and enjoyed themselves quite independently of her, making use of the excellent ice and the fine weather.
Nikolai Shcherbatsky, Kitty’s cousin, in a short jacket and tight trousers, was sitting on a bench with his skates on, and, seeing Levin, shouted to him:
“Ah, the first skater in Russia! Have you been here long? The ice is excellent; come on, put your skates on.”

“I haven’t even got any skates,” answered Levin, marvelling at this boldness and ease in her presence, and not for a second losing sight of her, though he did not look at her. He felt that the sun was coming closer to him. She was at a corner and, setting her narrow feet in their high boots at a blunt angle, evidently timid, was skating towards him. A boy in Russian dress, waving his arms desperately and bending low to the ice, was overtaking her. She did not skate quite steadily; taking her hands out of the little muff that hung on a cord, she held them ready, and, looking at Levin, whom she had recognized, she smiled at him and at her own fear. When the turn was over, she gave herself a push with her springy little foot and glided straight up to Shcherbatsky; and, catching hold of him with one hand, she nodded to Levin, smiling. She was more beautiful than he had imagined her.

When he thought of her, he could picture all of her vividly to himself, especially the charm of that small fair head, with its expression of childlike clearness and kindness, set so freely on her shapely girlish shoulders. The childlike look of her face, together with the delicate beauty of her figure, made up her special charm, which he remembered well; but what always struck him in her, like something unexpected, was the expression of her eyes, gentle, calm and truthful, and above all her smile, which always carried Levin into an enchanted world, where he felt himself touched and softened, as he could remember himself on rare days of his early childhood.
“Have you been here long?” she said, giving him her hand. “Thank you,” she added, when he picked up the handkerchief that had fallen from her muff.

“I? I’ve only just come, I came yesterday… today, I mean,” answered Levin, who in his agitation had not at once understood her question. “I meant to call on you,” he said; and at once, remembering with what intention he had been looking for her, he was confused and blushed. “I didn’t know you skated, and skated so well.”
She looked at him attentively, as though wanting to understand the cause of his confusion.
“Your praise is worth having. There is a tradition here that you are the best skater,” she said, brushing off with her little black-gloved hand the needles of hoar-frost that had fallen on her muff.
“Yes, at one time I skated with passion; I wanted to reach perfection.”
“You do everything with passion, it seems,” she said, smiling. “I so want to see how you skate. Do put on some skates, and let us skate together.”
“Skate together! Can it be possible?” thought Levin, looking at her.
“I’ll put them on at once,” he said.
And he went off to put on skates.

“You haven’t been to see us for a long time, sir,” said the attendant, holding up his foot and screwing on the heel. “Since you, there hasn’t been a single master among the gentlemen. Will that be all right?” he said, tightening the strap.

“All right, all right, quickly, please,” answered Levin, with difficulty holding back the smile of happiness that came out on his face in spite of him. “Yes,” he thought, “this is life, this is happiness! Together, she said, let us skate together. Shall I tell her now? But it’s precisely because I’m happy now that I’m afraid to tell her, happy if only with hope… And then?… But I must! I must, I must! Away with weakness!”

Levin stood up, took off his overcoat and, taking a run over the rough ice by the hut, came out onto the smooth ice and glided along without effort, as though quickening, shortening and steering his course by will alone. He came up to her timidly, but again her smile calmed him.
She gave him her hand, and they went side by side, gathering speed; and the faster they went, the more tightly she pressed his hand.
“With you I should learn sooner; for some reason I feel sure of you,” she said to him.

“And I feel sure of myself when you lean on me,” he said, but at once took fright at what he had said and blushed. And indeed, as soon as he had spoken these words, suddenly, as when the sun goes behind a cloud, her face lost all its warmth, and Levin recognized the familiar play of her face that meant an effort of thought: a little wrinkle swelled on her smooth forehead.
“Is anything troubling you? But I have no right to ask,” he said quickly.
“Why not?… No, nothing is troubling me,” she answered coldly, and at once added: “Have you seen Mademoiselle Linon?”
“Not yet.”
“Go to her; she is so fond of you.”

“What is this? I have upset her. Lord, help me!” thought Levin, and he skated off to the old Frenchwoman with grey ringlets who was sitting on a bench. Smiling and showing her false teeth, she met him like an old friend.

“Yes, here we are growing up,” she said to him, indicating Kitty with her eyes, “and growing old. The tiny bear has grown big already!” the Frenchwoman went on, laughing, and she reminded him of his joke about the three young ladies, whom he used to call the three bears from the English fairy tale. “Do you remember, you used to say that?”
He decidedly did not remember it, but she had been laughing at that joke for ten years or so and loved it.
“Well, go along, go and skate. Our Kitty has learned to skate well, hasn’t she?”

When Levin skated up to Kitty again, her face was no longer stern, her eyes looked at him just as truthfully and kindly; but it seemed to Levin that there was in her kindness a special, deliberately calm tone. And he felt sad. After talking about her old governess and her oddities, she asked him about his life.
“Don’t you really find it dull in the country in winter?” she said.

“No, not dull; I am very busy,” he said, feeling that she was bringing him under her calm tone, out of which he would not have the strength to break, just as it had been at the beginning of the winter.
“Have you come for long?” Kitty asked him.

“I don’t know,” he answered, not thinking of what he was saying. The thought came to him that if he gave in to this tone of calm friendship of hers he would go away again having settled nothing, and he decided to rebel.
“How can you not know?”
“I don’t know. It depends on you,” he said, and was at once horrified at his own words.

Whether she did not hear his words or did not want to hear them, she seemed to stumble, tapped her foot twice, and hurriedly skated away from him. She skated up to Mlle Linon, said something to her, and made for the hut where the ladies took off their skates.
“My God, what have I done! Lord my God! Help me, teach me,” said Levin, praying, and at the same time feeling a need for violent movement, he took a run and cut outer and inner circles.

At that moment one of the young men, the best of the new skaters, with a cigarette in his mouth and his skates on, came out of the coffee-house and, taking a run, went down the steps on his skates, clattering and bouncing. He flew down and, without even changing the easy position of his arms, glided away over the ice.
“Ah, that’s a new trick!” said Levin, and at once ran up to the top to do this new trick.
“Don’t kill yourself, it takes practice!” Nikolai Shcherbatsky shouted to him.

Levin went up onto the landing, took as long a run as he could from the top, and went off down, keeping his balance with his arms in the unfamiliar movement. On the last step he caught his foot, but, barely touching the ice with his hand, he made a strong movement, recovered himself and, laughing, glided on.

“Splendid, dear man,” thought Kitty at that moment, coming out of the hut with Mlle Linon and looking at him with a smile of quiet tenderness, as at a beloved brother. “And am I really to blame? Have I really done anything wrong? They say: flirting. I know it is not he whom I love; but still I am happy with him, and he is so splendid. Only why did he say that?…” she thought.

Seeing Kitty leaving, and her mother meeting her on the steps, Levin, flushed after the quick movement, stopped and grew thoughtful. He took off his skates and caught up with mother and daughter at the gate of the gardens.
“Very glad to see you,” said the princess. “We are at home on Thursdays, as always.”
“Today, then?”
“We shall be very glad to see you,” said the princess drily.
This dryness upset Kitty, and she could not resist the wish to smooth over her mother’s coldness. She turned her head and said with a smile:
“Goodbye till then.”

At that moment Stepan Arkadyich, his hat on one side, his face and eyes shining, was coming into the gardens like a cheerful conqueror. But, on reaching his mother-in-law, he answered her questions about Dolly’s health with a sad and guilty face. After talking quietly and dejectedly with his mother-in-law, he straightened his chest and took Levin’s arm.
“Well, shall we go?” he asked. “I kept thinking about you, and I am very, very glad you have come,” he said, looking him in the eyes with a significant air.
“Let’s go, let’s go,” answered the happy Levin, who still could not stop hearing the sound of the voice that had said “Goodbye till then” and seeing the smile with which it had been said.
“To the Angleterre or the Hermitage?”
“I don’t mind.”

“Well, the Angleterre, then,” said Stepan Arkadyich, choosing the Angleterre because he owed more there than at the Hermitage. For that reason he thought it wrong to avoid that hotel. “Have you got a cab? Good, because I sent my carriage away.”

The friends were silent all the way. Levin was thinking about what that change of expression on Kitty’s face had meant, and now he assured himself that there was hope, now he fell into despair and saw clearly that his hope was mad; and all the while he felt himself quite another man, not like the one he had been before her smile and her “goodbye till then”.
On the way Stepan Arkadyich was composing the menu.
“You like turbot, don’t you?” he said to Levin as they drove up.
“What?” Levin asked again. “Turbot? Yes, I love turbot terribly.”
## Chapter X

When Levin went into the hotel with Oblonsky, he could not help noticing a certain peculiarity of expression, a kind of restrained radiance, on the face and in the whole figure of Stepan Arkadyich. Oblonsky took off his overcoat and, with his hat tilted over one ear, went through into the dining-room, giving orders to the Tatar waiters in tailcoats with napkins over their arms, who clung to him. Bowing right and left to acquaintances who turned up here too, as everywhere, and greeted him joyfully, he went up to the buffet, took a little fish after his vodka, and said something to the painted Frenchwoman sitting at the counter, all ribbons, lace and ringlets, that made even this Frenchwoman laugh sincerely. Levin did not drink any vodka only because this Frenchwoman offended him: she seemed made up entirely of other people’s hair, poudre de riz and vinaigre de toilette. He moved hastily away from her, as from a dirty place. His whole soul was overflowing with the memory of Kitty, and a smile of triumph and happiness shone in his eyes.

“This way, your excellency, if you please; no one will disturb you here, your excellency,” said a particularly clinging old Tatar, whitish, with broad hips and the tails of his coat parting over them. “Your hat, your excellency, if you please,” he said to Levin, attending to Stepan Arkadyich’s guest too, as a mark of respect to Stepan Arkadyich.

In an instant he had spread a fresh cloth over the round table, which already had a cloth on it, under a bronze wall-lamp, drew up the velvet chairs, and stood before Stepan Arkadyich with a napkin and the bill of fare in his hands, awaiting orders.
“If you wish, your excellency, a private room will be free directly: Prince Golitsyn with a lady. Fresh oysters have come in.”
“Ah! Oysters.”
Stepan Arkadyich thought for a moment.
“Shall we change the plan, Levin?” he said, stopping his finger on the bill of fare. And his face expressed serious perplexity. “Are the oysters good? Mind, now!”
“Flensburg ones, your excellency; there are no Ostend ones.”
“Flensburg is all very well, but are they fresh?”
“They came in yesterday, sir.”
“Well then, shall we begin with oysters, and then change the whole plan? Eh?”
“I don’t mind. For me the best thing of all is cabbage soup and kasha; but they won’t have that here.”
“Kasha à la russe, would you like?” said the Tatar, bending over Levin like a nurse over a child.

“No, seriously, whatever you choose will be good. I’ve been skating and I’m hungry. And don’t think,” he added, noticing a look of displeasure on Oblonsky’s face, “that I don’t appreciate your choice. I shall enjoy a good dinner.”

“I should think so! Say what you like, it is one of the pleasures of life,” said Stepan Arkadyich. “Well then, my good fellow, give us two dozen oysters, or that’s too few, three dozen; soup with vegetables…”
“Printanière,” the Tatar put in. But Stepan Arkadyich evidently did not want to give him the pleasure of calling the dishes by their French names.
“With vegetables, you know? Then turbot with a thick sauce, then… roast beef; and mind it’s good. And capons, perhaps, and then some preserved fruit.”
