The Tatar, remembering Stepan Arkadyich’s way of not calling the dishes by the French bill of fare, did not repeat after him, but gave himself the pleasure of repeating the whole order from the bill: “Soupe printanière, turbot sauce Beaumarchais, poularde à l’estragon, macédoine de fruits…” and at once, as if on springs, laying down one bound bill of fare and snatching up another, the wine list, he handed it to Stepan Arkadyich.
“What shall we drink?”
“Whatever you like, only not much; champagne,” said Levin.
“What? To begin with? But, after all, why not. Do you like the white seal?”
“Cachet blanc,” the Tatar put in.
“Well, bring us that brand with the oysters, and then we shall see.”
“Very good, sir. And what table wine would you like?”
“Bring Nuits. No, better the classic Chablis.”
“Very good, sir. Will you have your usual cheese?”
“Yes, Parmesan. Or do you like another?”
“No, it’s all the same to me,” said Levin, unable to hold back his smiles.

And the Tatar, the tails of his coat flying over his broad hips, ran off, and five minutes later flew in with a dish of opened oysters on their mother-of-pearl shells and a bottle between his fingers.
Stepan Arkadyich crumpled the starched napkin, tucked it into his waistcoat, and, settling his arms comfortably, set to on the oysters.

“Not bad,” he said, tearing the slippery oysters from their pearly shells with a little silver fork and swallowing them one after another. “Not bad,” he repeated, lifting his moist, shining eyes now to Levin, now to the Tatar.

Levin ate the oysters too, though white bread and cheese would have pleased him more. But he was admiring Oblonsky. Even the Tatar, who had unscrewed the cork and was pouring the sparkling wine into the wide, thin glasses, kept glancing at Stepan Arkadyich with a noticeable smile of pleasure as he set his white tie straight.
“You don’t much like oysters?” said Stepan Arkadyich, emptying his glass. “Or are you worried about something? Eh?”

He wanted Levin to be cheerful. But it was not that Levin was not cheerful; he was ill at ease. With what was in his soul, he felt uneasy and awkward in a restaurant, among private rooms where people dined with ladies, amid all this running about and bustle; these surroundings of bronzes, mirrors, gaslight, Tatars, all of it offended him. He was afraid of soiling what filled his soul to overflowing.
“I? Yes, I am worried; but besides that, all this makes me feel awkward,” he said. “You can’t imagine how wild all this is to me, a countryman, like the nails of that gentleman I saw in your office…”
“Yes, I saw that poor Grinevich’s nails interested you very much,” said Stepan Arkadyich, laughing.

“I can’t help it,” answered Levin. “Do try to get inside me, to take the countryman’s point of view. In the country we try to keep our hands in such a state that it is convenient to work with them; for that we cut our nails, and sometimes roll up our sleeves. And here people purposely let their nails grow as long as they will stay on, and hook on saucers by way of cuff-links, so that they can’t do anything at all with their hands.”
Stepan Arkadyich smiled merrily.
“Yes, it is a sign that he has no need of rough labour. It’s his mind that works…”

“Perhaps. But still it is wild to me, just as it is wild to me now that we countrymen try to eat our fill as quickly as possible, so as to be able to do our work, while you and I try to put off eating our fill as long as possible, and to that end we eat oysters…”
“Why, of course,” Stepan Arkadyich took him up. “But that is just the aim of civilization: to make everything a source of enjoyment.”
“Well, if that is the aim, I would rather be a savage.”
“You are a savage as it is. All you Levins are savages.”
Levin sighed. He remembered his brother Nikolai, and he felt ashamed and pained, and frowned; but Oblonsky began speaking of a subject that at once drew him away.
“Well, are you going to our people this evening, to the Shcherbatskys, I mean?” he said, pushing away the empty rough shells, drawing the cheese towards him, and with his eyes shining significantly.
“Yes, I shall certainly go,” answered Levin. “Though it seemed to me that the princess invited me unwillingly.”

“What nonsense! It’s her manner… Come on, my dear fellow, the soup!… It’s her manner, the grande dame,” said Stepan Arkadyich. “I shall come too, but I have to go to a choir rehearsal at Countess Banina’s first. Well, how can you say you’re not a savage? How else can one explain your suddenly vanishing from Moscow? The Shcherbatskys kept asking me about you, as though I ought to know. And I know only one thing: you always do what nobody else does.”
“Yes,” said Levin, slowly and with emotion. “You’re right, I am a savage. Only my savagery lies not in my having gone away but in my having come back now. Now I have come…”
“Oh, what a lucky man you are!” Stepan Arkadyich took him up, looking into Levin’s eyes.
“Why?”
“‘I know a mettled horse by the brand upon his hide, and a youth in love I know by the look in his eyes,’” declaimed Stepan Arkadyich. “Everything is before you.”
“And is it all behind you, then?”
“No, not behind me, but you have the future, and I have the present, and the present only so-so, a bit of this and a bit of that.”
“How so?”

“Oh, not good. Well, I don’t want to talk about myself, and besides, it can’t all be explained,” said Stepan Arkadyich. “So what have you come to Moscow for?… Here, take this away!” he called to the Tatar.
“Can’t you guess?” answered Levin, not taking his eyes, which shone from the depths, off Stepan Arkadyich.
“I can guess, but I can’t begin to talk about it. By that alone you can see whether I guess right or wrong,” said Stepan Arkadyich, looking at Levin with a subtle smile.
“Well, what do you say to me?” said Levin in a trembling voice, feeling that all the muscles of his face were trembling. “How do you look at it?”
Stepan Arkadyich slowly drank his glass of Chablis, not taking his eyes off Levin.
“I?” said Stepan Arkadyich. “There is nothing I should like better than that, nothing. It is the best thing that could happen.”
“But you are not mistaken? You know what we are talking about?” said Levin, fastening his eyes on his companion. “You think it is possible?”
“I think it is possible. Why should it be impossible?”
“No, do you really think it is possible? No, tell me everything you think! Well, and if, if a refusal awaits me?… And I am even sure…”
“Why do you think that?” said Stepan Arkadyich, smiling at his agitation.
“That’s how it seems to me sometimes. It would be terrible, you know, both for me and for her.”
“Well, in any case there is nothing terrible in it for the girl. Every girl is proud of a proposal.”
“Yes, every girl, but not she.”

Stepan Arkadyich smiled. He knew this feeling of Levin’s so well; he knew that for him all the girls in the world were divided into two sorts: one sort was all the girls in the world except her, and these had every human weakness and were very ordinary girls; the other sort was she alone, who had no weaknesses at all and was above everything human.
“Wait, take some sauce,” he said, holding back Levin’s hand, which was pushing the sauce away.
Levin obediently helped himself to sauce, but he would not let Stepan Arkadyich eat.

“No, wait, wait,” he said. “You must understand that for me this is a question of life and death. I have never spoken of it to anyone. And there is no one I can speak to about it as I can to you. You and I are strangers in everything, you know: different tastes, views, everything; but I know that you love me and understand me, and that is why I love you terribly. But for God’s sake be perfectly frank.”

“I am telling you what I think,” said Stepan Arkadyich, smiling. “But I’ll tell you more: my wife is the most wonderful woman…” Stepan Arkadyich sighed, remembering how things stood with his wife, and, after a moment’s silence, went on: “She has the gift of foresight. She sees through people; but that is not all; she knows what is going to happen, especially in the matter of marriages. She foretold, for instance, that Princess Shakhovskaya would marry Brenteln. No one would believe it, but so it turned out. And she is on your side.”
“How do you mean?”
“I mean that not only does she love you; she says that Kitty will certainly be your wife.”
At these words Levin’s face suddenly lit up with a smile, the kind that is close to tears of tenderness.
“She says that!” cried Levin. “I always said she was a darling, your wife. Well, that’s enough, enough talking about it,” he said, getting up from his seat.
“All right, but do sit down; here’s the soup.”
But Levin could not sit. He walked twice with his firm steps up and down the little cage of a room, blinked his eyes so that his tears should not be seen, and only then sat down at the table again.

“You must understand,” he said, “that this is not love. I have been in love, but this is not that. It is not my feeling, but some outside force that has taken possession of me. I went away, you see, because I decided that it could not be, you understand, like a happiness that does not happen on earth; but I have struggled with myself, and I see that without it there is no life. And it must be decided…”
“Then why did you go away?”

“Ah, wait! Ah, so many thoughts! So much to ask! Listen. You can’t imagine what you have done for me by what you have said. I am so happy that I have even become horrid; I have forgotten everything… I learned today that my brother Nikolai… you know, he is here… I had forgotten about him too. It seems to me that he is happy too. It is a kind of madness. But one thing is terrible… You have married, you know this feeling… The terrible thing is that we, who are old, with a past already… not of love, but of sins… suddenly draw close to a pure, innocent being; it is loathsome, and so one cannot help feeling unworthy.”
“Well, you haven’t many sins.”
“Ah, all the same,” said Levin, “all the same: ‘and with loathing reading over my life, I tremble and I curse, and bitterly complain…’ Yes.”
“What can one do? That is how the world is made,” said Stepan Arkadyich.
“There is one comfort, as in that prayer I have always loved: forgive me not according to my deserts, but according to Thy mercy. And so she too can only forgive.”
## Chapter XI
Levin drank his glass, and they were silent for a while.
“There is one more thing I must tell you. Do you know Vronsky?” Stepan Arkadyich asked Levin.
“No, I don’t. Why do you ask?”
“Bring another,” said Stepan Arkadyich, turning to the Tatar, who was filling up their glasses and hovering about them precisely when he was not wanted.
“Why should I know Vronsky?”
“The reason you should know Vronsky is that he is one of your rivals.”
“And what is Vronsky?” said Levin, and his face changed suddenly from that childishly rapturous expression which Oblonsky had just been admiring to an angry and unpleasant one.

“Vronsky is one of the sons of Count Kirill Ivanovich Vronsky, and one of the finest specimens of the gilded youth of Petersburg. I got to know him in Tver, when I was in the service there and he came for the recruiting. Terribly rich, handsome, great connections, an aide-de-camp, and at the same time a very nice, good-natured fellow. But more than just a good-natured fellow. As I have come to know him here, he is both cultivated and very clever; he is a man who will go far.”
Levin frowned and was silent.
“Well, he turned up here soon after you left, and, as I understand it, he is head over ears in love with Kitty, and you understand that her mother…”
“Excuse me, but I don’t understand anything,” said Levin, scowling gloomily. And at once he remembered his brother Nikolai, and how vile he was to have been able to forget him.

“Wait, wait,” said Stepan Arkadyich, smiling and touching his hand. “I have told you what I know, and I repeat that in this delicate, tender business, as far as one can guess, it seems to me that the chances are on your side.”
Levin leaned back in his chair; his face was pale.
“But I would advise you to settle the matter as quickly as possible,” Oblonsky went on, filling up his glass.
“No, thank you, I can’t drink any more,” said Levin, pushing his glass away. “I shall be drunk… Well, and how are you getting on?” he went on, evidently wanting to change the subject.

“One word more: in any case I advise you to settle the question soon. I don’t advise you to speak tonight,” said Stepan Arkadyich. “Go tomorrow morning, in the classic way, and make your proposal, and God bless you…”
“Why is it you kept meaning to come and shoot with me? Come in the spring, for the evening flight of the woodcock,” said Levin.

Now he repented with all his soul that he had begun this conversation with Stepan Arkadyich. His special feeling had been profaned by talk of the rivalry of some Petersburg officer, by Stepan Arkadyich’s suppositions and advice.
Stepan Arkadyich smiled. He understood what was going on in Levin’s soul.

“I’ll come some time,” he said. “Yes, my dear fellow, women are the screw on which everything turns. My own affairs are bad, very bad. And all because of women. Tell me frankly,” he went on, taking out a cigar and keeping one hand on his glass, “give me some advice.”
“But about what?”
“About this. Suppose you are married, you love your wife, but you have been carried away by another woman…”
“Excuse me, but I simply don’t understand that; it’s just as if… just as I can’t understand how I could now, after eating my fill here, walk past a baker’s shop and steal a roll.”
Stepan Arkadyich’s eyes shone more than usual.
“Why not? A roll sometimes smells so good that one can’t resist.

> Heavenly it is when I have conquered
> All my earthly appetite;
> But if I should fail to conquer,
> Still I’ve had a fine delight!”
As he said this, Stepan Arkadyich smiled subtly. Levin too could not help smiling.

“Yes, but joking aside,” Oblonsky went on. “You must understand that the woman is a sweet, gentle, loving creature, poor, alone, and she has sacrificed everything. Now, when the thing is done, you understand, can one really abandon her? Suppose we part, so as not to destroy family life; but is one not to pity her, not to provide for her, not to soften things for her?”

“Well, you must excuse me. You know, for me all women are divided into two sorts… that is, no… rather: there are women, and there are… I have never seen any charming fallen creatures and never shall, and women like that painted Frenchwoman at the counter, with her ringlets, are vermin to me, and all fallen women are the same.”
“And the one in the Gospel?”

“Oh, stop it! Christ would never have said those words if he had known how they would be abused. Out of the whole Gospel those are the only words people remember. However, I am saying not what I think but what I feel. I have a loathing for fallen women. You are afraid of spiders, and I am afraid of these vermin. You have probably never studied spiders and don’t know their habits: it’s the same with me.”

“It’s all very well for you to talk like that; it’s like that gentleman in Dickens who tosses every awkward question over his right shoulder with his left hand. But denying a fact is not an answer. What is to be done, you tell me, what is to be done? Your wife grows old, and you are full of life. Before you know where you are, you feel that you cannot love your wife with love, however much you may respect her. And then suddenly love turns up, and you are lost, lost!” Stepan Arkadyich said with dejected despair.
Levin smiled.
“Yes, lost,” Oblonsky went on. “But what is to be done?”
“Don’t steal rolls.”
Stepan Arkadyich laughed.

“Oh, you moralist! But you must understand, there are two women: one insists only on her rights, and those rights are your love, which you cannot give her; and the other sacrifices everything to you and demands nothing. What are you to do? How are you to act? There is a terrible drama here.”

“If you want my confession on that, I will tell you that I don’t believe there is any drama here. And here is why. To my mind, love… both kinds of love, which, you remember, Plato defines in his Symposium, both kinds serve as a touchstone for men. Some men understand only the one, others the other. And those who understand only the non-Platonic love talk of drama for nothing. With that kind of love there can be no drama at all. ‘I humbly thank you for the pleasure, my respects,’ and that is the whole drama. And for Platonic love there can be no drama, because in such a love everything is clear and pure, because…”
At that moment Levin remembered his own sins and the inner struggle he had lived through. And he added unexpectedly:
“But then, perhaps you are right. It may very well be… But I don’t know, I really don’t know.”

“There, you see,” said Stepan Arkadyich, “you are a very whole man. That is your quality and your failing. You have a whole character yourself, and you want all of life to be made up of whole things, and that is not how it is. You despise public service, for instance, because you want the work always to correspond to its aim, and that is not how it is. You want, too, every man’s activity always to have an aim, and love and family life always to be one and the same. And that is not how it is. All the variety, all the charm, all the beauty of life is made up of light and shade.”
Levin sighed and made no answer. He was thinking of his own affairs and not listening to Oblonsky.

And suddenly they both felt that, though they were friends, though they had dined together and drunk wine that should have drawn them still closer, each was thinking only of his own affairs, and neither cared about the other. Oblonsky had more than once experienced this extreme division instead of closeness that happens after dinner, and he knew what to do in such cases.

“The bill!” he called, and went into the next room, where he at once met an aide-de-camp he knew and got into a conversation with him about an actress and the man who kept her. And at once, in his talk with the aide-de-camp, Oblonsky felt relief and rest from his conversation with Levin, who always drew him into too great a strain of mind and heart.

When the Tatar appeared with the bill for twenty-six roubles and some kopecks, plus something for himself, Levin, who at another time, as a countryman, would have been horrified at his share of fourteen roubles, now paid no attention to it, paid, and went home to change and go to the Shcherbatskys’, where his fate would be decided.
## Part One · Chapter XII

Princess Kitty Shcherbatskaya was eighteen. This was her first winter out in society. Her success in society was greater than that of both her elder sisters, and greater even than the princess had expected. Not only were almost all the young men who danced at the Moscow balls in love with Kitty, but already in this first winter two serious matches had presented themselves: Levin, and, immediately after his departure, Count Vronsky.

Levin’s appearance at the beginning of the winter, his frequent visits and his evident love for Kitty had given rise to the first serious conversations between Kitty’s parents about her future, and to disputes between the prince and the princess. The prince was on Levin’s side; he said he wished for nothing better for Kitty. The princess, with the habit women have of going round a question, said that Kitty was too young, that Levin gave no sign of having serious intentions, that Kitty felt no attachment to him, and other arguments; but she did not say the main thing, which was that she was waiting for a better match for her daughter, that Levin was not to her liking, and that she did not understand him. When Levin suddenly went away, the princess was glad, and said triumphantly to her husband: “You see, I was right.” And when Vronsky appeared she was gladder still, confirmed in her opinion that Kitty must make not merely a good match but a brilliant one.

For the mother there could be no comparison between Vronsky and Levin. The mother disliked Levin’s strange and abrupt opinions, and his awkwardness in society, founded, as she supposed, on pride, and his life in the country, which by her notions was somehow savage, occupied with cattle and peasants; and she disliked very much that he, in love with her daughter, had been coming to the house for six weeks as though waiting for something, watching, as though afraid that it would be too great an honour if he proposed, and had not understood that a man who comes to a house where there is a marriageable girl must declare himself. And suddenly, without declaring himself, he had gone away. “It’s a good thing he is so unattractive that Kitty didn’t fall in love with him,” thought the mother.
Vronsky satisfied all the mother’s wishes. Very rich, clever, of good family, on the way to a brilliant career in the army and at court, and a fascinating man. Nothing better could be wished for.

At balls Vronsky openly courted Kitty, danced with her and came to the house; so there could be no doubt of the seriousness of his intentions. And yet, in spite of this, the mother spent the whole winter in terrible anxiety and agitation.

The princess herself had married thirty years before, through an aunt’s matchmaking. The bridegroom, about whom everything was known beforehand, came, saw the bride and was seen; the matchmaking aunt found out and passed on the impression made on both sides; the impression was good; then, on an appointed day, the expected proposal was made to the parents and accepted. It all happened very easily and simply. At least so it seemed to the princess. But with her own daughters she had found out how far from easy and simple it is, this business that seems so ordinary, the marrying off of daughters. How many fears she had lived through, how many thoughts she had thought over, how much money had been spent, how many clashes with her husband there had been over the marrying of the two elder ones, Darya and Natalya! Now, with the youngest coming out, the same fears were being lived through, the same doubts, and still greater quarrels with her husband than over the elder ones. The old prince, like all fathers, was particularly scrupulous about the honour and purity of his daughters; he was unreasonably jealous over his daughters, and especially over Kitty, who was his favourite, and at every step he made scenes with the princess for compromising their daughter. The princess had grown used to this with the first daughters, but now she felt that the prince’s scrupulousness had more grounds. She saw that a great deal had changed lately in the ways of society, that a mother’s duties had become still harder. She saw that girls of Kitty’s age formed some sort of societies, went to some sort of courses, mixed freely with men, drove about the streets alone; many of them did not curtsey, and, above all, they were all firmly convinced that choosing a husband was their own business and not their parents’. “Girls are not married off nowadays the way they used to be,” all these young girls thought and said, and so did all the old people too. But how girls were married off nowadays the princess could not find out from anyone. The French custom, that parents decide their children’s fate, was not accepted; it was condemned. The English custom, the complete freedom of the girl, was not accepted either, and was impossible in Russian society. The Russian custom of matchmaking was considered something monstrous; everyone laughed at it, the princess herself included. But how girls ought to marry and be married, nobody knew. Everyone with whom the princess happened to discuss it said one thing to her: “Mercy, in our day it is time to give up these old ways. After all, it is the young people who are getting married, not the parents; so the young people must be left to arrange things as they see fit.” But it was all very well for people who had no daughters to say that; the princess understood that, as they came together, her daughter might fall in love, and fall in love with someone who did not want to marry, or with someone who was not fit to be a husband. And however much it was impressed on the princess that in our day young people must arrange their fate for themselves, she could not believe it, any more than she could have believed that, at any time whatever, the best toys for five-year-old children must be loaded pistols. And so the princess was more anxious over Kitty than she had been over the elder daughters.

Now she was afraid that Vronsky would confine himself to merely courting her daughter. She saw that her daughter was already in love with him, but she comforted herself with the thought that he was an honourable man and so would not do that. And yet she knew how easy it is, with today’s freedom of manners, to turn a girl’s head, and how lightly men in general look on that offence. The week before, Kitty had told her mother of a conversation she had had with Vronsky during the mazurka. This conversation had partly reassured the princess, but she could not be entirely at ease. Vronsky had told Kitty that he and his brother were both so used to submitting to their mother in everything that they would never decide on anything important without consulting her. “And now I am waiting, as for a special happiness, for my mother to arrive from Petersburg,” he had said.

Kitty told this without attaching any significance to the words. But her mother understood it differently. She knew that the old lady was expected any day, she knew that the old lady would be pleased with her son’s choice, and she found it strange that he was not proposing for fear of offending his mother; however, she so wanted the marriage itself, and above all relief from her anxieties, that she believed it. Bitter as it now was for the princess to see the unhappiness of her eldest daughter, Dolly, who was preparing to leave her husband, her agitation over the deciding of her youngest daughter’s fate absorbed all her feelings. Today, with the appearance of Levin, a new anxiety had been added. She was afraid that her daughter, who had at one time, as it seemed to her, felt something for Levin, might out of excessive honesty refuse Vronsky, and in general that Levin’s arrival might complicate and delay a matter so near its conclusion.
“Has he been here long?” said the princess of Levin, when they got home.
“Since today, maman.”
“There is one thing I want to say…” the princess began, and from her seriously animated face Kitty guessed what it would be about.
“Mama,” she said, flushing and turning quickly towards her, “please, please don’t say anything about that. I know, I know everything.”
She wished for the same thing as her mother, but her mother’s motives for wishing it offended her.
“I only want to say that, having given hope to one…”
“Mama, darling, for God’s sake don’t speak. It is so dreadful to talk about it.”
“I won’t, I won’t,” said the mother, seeing tears in her daughter’s eyes; “but one thing, my love: you promised me that you would have no secrets from me. You won’t?”

“Never, mama, none at all,” answered Kitty, blushing and looking straight into her mother’s face. “But I have nothing to tell now. I… I… if I wanted to, I don’t know what to say or how… I don’t know…”

“No, she can’t tell an untruth with those eyes,” thought the mother, smiling at her agitation and her happiness. The princess was smiling at how enormous and significant what was now happening in her soul seemed to her, poor little thing.
## Chapter XIII
After dinner, until the beginning of the evening, Kitty felt something like what a young man feels before a battle. Her heart beat violently, and her thoughts could not settle on anything.

She felt that this evening, when the two of them would meet for the first time, must be decisive in her fate. And she kept picturing them to herself, now each separately, now both together. When she thought of the past, she dwelt with pleasure, with tenderness, on her memories of her relations with Levin. Memories of childhood and of Levin’s friendship with her dead brother gave a special poetic charm to her relations with him. His love for her, of which she was sure, was flattering and joyful to her. And it was easy for her to remember Levin. With her memories of Vronsky, on the contrary, something awkward was mixed, though he was in the highest degree a calm man of the world; as though there were some falseness, not in him, he was very simple and nice, but in herself; whereas with Levin she felt herself perfectly simple and clear. But then, as soon as she thought of the future with Vronsky, a prospect of brilliant happiness rose before her; with Levin the future seemed misty.

Going upstairs to dress for the evening and looking in the mirror, she noticed with joy that this was one of her good days and that she was in full possession of all her powers, which she so needed for what lay ahead: she felt in herself an outward calm and a free grace of movement.

At half past seven, just as she came down into the drawing-room, the footman announced: “Konstantin Dmitrich Levin.” The princess was still in her room, and the prince had not come out. “So it is,” thought Kitty, and all the blood rushed to her heart. Glancing in the mirror, she was horrified at how pale she was.

Now she knew for certain that he had come early precisely to find her alone and to propose. And only now, for the first time, did the whole matter appear to her from quite another side, a new one. Only now did she understand that the question concerned not her alone, whom she would be happy with and whom she loved, but that this very minute she must wound a man she loved. And wound him cruelly… For what? Because he, the dear man, loved her, was in love with her. But there was nothing to be done; it had to be so, it must be so.

“My God, must I really tell him myself?” she thought. “What shall I say to him? Am I really to tell him that I don’t love him? That would be untrue. What shall I say to him? Say that I love another? No, that is impossible. I’ll go away, I’ll go away.”

She was already going towards the door when she heard his steps. “No! It’s not honest. What have I to be afraid of? I have done nothing wrong. What will be, will be! I shall tell the truth. And with him one can’t feel awkward. Here he is,” she said to herself, seeing his whole strong and timid figure, with his shining eyes fixed on her. She looked him straight in the face, as though begging him for mercy, and gave him her hand.

“I have come at the wrong time, I think; too early,” he said, glancing round the empty drawing-room. When he saw that his expectations had come true, that nothing prevented him from speaking out, his face became gloomy.
“Oh, no,” said Kitty, and sat down at the table.
“But that was just what I wanted, to find you alone,” he began, not sitting down and not looking at her, so as not to lose his courage.
“Mama will be out in a moment. She was very tired yesterday. Yesterday…”
She was talking without knowing herself what her lips were saying, and without taking her pleading, caressing eyes off him.
He looked at her; she blushed and fell silent.
“I told you that I didn’t know whether I had come for long… that it depended on you…”
She bent her head lower and lower, not knowing herself what she would answer to what was coming.

“That it depended on you,” he repeated. “I wanted to say… I wanted to say… That is what I came for… that… to be my wife!” he brought out, not knowing himself what he was saying; but, feeling that the most terrible thing had been said, he stopped and looked at her.

She was breathing heavily, not looking at him. She felt rapture. Her soul was overflowing with happiness. She had never expected that his declared love would make such a strong impression on her. But this lasted only an instant. She remembered Vronsky. She raised her clear, truthful eyes to Levin, and, seeing his desperate face, answered hurriedly:
“That cannot be… forgive me…”
How close to him she had been a minute before, how important to his life! And how alien and far from him she had become now!
“It could not have been otherwise,” he said, not looking at her.
He bowed and was about to leave.
## Chapter XIV

But at that very moment the princess came out. Horror showed on her face when she saw them alone and their upset faces. Levin bowed to her and said nothing. Kitty was silent and did not raise her eyes. “Thank God, she has refused him,” thought the mother, and her face lit up with the usual smile with which she greeted her guests on Thursdays. She sat down and began asking Levin about his life in the country. He sat down again, waiting for the guests to arrive so as to leave unnoticed.
Five minutes later a friend of Kitty’s came in, Countess Nordston, who had married the winter before.

She was a dry, sallow, sickly, nervous woman with shining black eyes. She loved Kitty, and her love for her, as the love of married women for girls always does, showed itself in a wish to marry Kitty according to her own ideal of happiness; and so she wished to marry her to Vronsky. Levin, whom she had often met at their house at the beginning of the winter, had always been disagreeable to her. Her constant and favourite occupation when she met him was to make fun of him.

“I love it when he looks down at me from the height of his greatness: either he breaks off his clever conversation with me because I am stupid, or he condescends. I like that very much: he condescends to me! I am very glad that he can’t stand me,” she would say of him.

She was right, because Levin really could not stand her and despised her for the very things she was proud of and counted to her credit: her nervousness, her refined contempt and indifference for everything coarse and everyday.

Between Countess Nordston and Levin there had been established that relationship, not uncommon in society, in which two people, outwardly remaining on friendly terms, despise each other so much that they cannot even treat each other seriously, and cannot even be offended by each other.
Countess Nordston at once pounced on Levin.

“Ah! Konstantin Dmitrich! You have come back to our depraved Babylon,” she said, giving him her tiny yellow hand and remembering his words, said some time at the beginning of the winter, that Moscow was Babylon. “Well, has Babylon reformed, or have you been corrupted?” she added, glancing round at Kitty with a smirk.

“I am very flattered, Countess, that you remember my words so well,” answered Levin, who had managed to recover himself and, from habit, at once fell into his jokingly hostile manner with Countess Nordston. “They must have a very strong effect on you.”
“Oh, of course! I write everything down. Well, Kitty, have you been skating again?…”

And she began talking to Kitty. However awkward it was for Levin to leave now, it was still easier for him to commit this awkwardness than to stay the whole evening and see Kitty, who glanced at him now and then and avoided his eyes. He was about to get up, but the princess, noticing that he was silent, turned to him.
“Have you come to Moscow for long? You are busy with the zemstvo, I believe, and can’t stay long.”
“No, Princess, I am no longer busy with the zemstvo,” he said. “I have come for a few days.”

“There is something special about him today,” thought Countess Nordston, peering into his stern, serious face; “somehow he isn’t getting drawn into his arguments. But I’ll bring him out. I do love making a fool of him in front of Kitty, and I shall.”

“Konstantin Dmitrich,” she said to him, “do explain to me, please, what it means (you know all about these things): in our village in Kaluga all the peasants and all the women have drunk away everything they had, and now they pay us nothing. What does that mean? You always praise the peasants so.”
At that moment another lady came into the room, and Levin got up.
“Excuse me, Countess, but I really know nothing about it and can tell you nothing,” he said, and looked round at the officer who was coming in behind the lady.

“That must be Vronsky,” thought Levin, and, to make sure, he glanced at Kitty. She had already had time to glance at Vronsky, and she looked round at Levin. And by that one glance of her eyes, which had lit up in spite of herself, Levin understood that she loved this man; understood it as surely as if she had told him so in words. But what sort of man was he?
Now, whether for good or ill, Levin could not help staying; he had to find out what sort of man it was whom she loved.

There are people who, on meeting a rival who has been lucky in anything whatever, are ready at once to turn away from everything good in him and to see only what is bad; and there are people who, on the contrary, wish above all to find in this lucky rival the qualities by which he has beaten them, and who look in him, with an aching pain in the heart, only for what is good. Levin was one of these. But it was not hard for him to find what was good and attractive in Vronsky. It struck him at once. Vronsky was a dark man, not tall, solidly built, with a good-natured, handsome, exceedingly calm and firm face. In his face and figure, from his close-cropped black hair and freshly shaved chin to his loose-fitting, brand-new uniform, everything was simple and at the same time elegant. Making way for the lady who was coming in, Vronsky went up to the princess and then to Kitty.

As he came up to her, his handsome eyes shone with particular tenderness, and with a barely noticeable smile, happy and modestly triumphant (so it seemed to Levin), bending over her respectfully and carefully, he held out his small but broad hand to her.
Having greeted everyone and said a few words, he sat down without once looking at Levin, who did not take his eyes off him.
“Allow me to introduce you,” said the princess, indicating Levin. “Konstantin Dmitrich Levin. Count Alexei Kirillovich Vronsky.”
Vronsky got up and, looking Levin in the eyes in a friendly way, shook his hand.
“I was to have dined with you this winter, I believe,” he said, smiling his simple and open smile, “but you went off to the country unexpectedly.”
“Konstantin Dmitrich despises and hates the town and us townspeople,” said Countess Nordston.
“My words must have a strong effect on you, since you remember them so well,” said Levin; and, remembering that he had already said that, he blushed.
Vronsky looked at Levin and at Countess Nordston and smiled.
“And are you always in the country?” he asked. “I should think it is dull in winter?”
“It isn’t dull if one has things to do, and one isn’t dull with oneself,” Levin answered sharply.
“I love the country,” said Vronsky, noticing Levin’s tone and pretending not to notice it.
“But I hope, Count, that you would not agree to live in the country always,” said Countess Nordston.

“I don’t know; I have never tried it for long. I have had a strange feeling,” he went on. “Nowhere have I missed the country so much, the Russian country, with bast shoes and peasants, as when I spent a winter with my mother in Nice. Nice is dull in itself, you know. And Naples and Sorrento are good only for a short time. And it is precisely there that Russia comes back so vividly, and precisely the country. They are just like…”
He was talking to both Kitty and Levin, moving his calm and friendly gaze from one to the other, and saying, evidently, whatever came into his head.
Noticing that Countess Nordston wanted to say something, he stopped without finishing what he had begun, and listened to her attentively.

The conversation did not flag for a minute, so that the old princess, who always kept two heavy guns in reserve in case there was nothing to talk about, classical against modern education, and universal military service, did not have to bring them out, and Countess Nordston did not get a chance to tease Levin.
Levin wanted to join in the general conversation and could not; saying to himself every minute, “Now I’ll go,” he did not go, but waited for something.
The conversation turned to table-turning and spirits, and Countess Nordston, who believed in spiritualism, began to tell of the wonders she had seen.
“Ah, Countess, you must take me, for God’s sake take me to them! I have never seen anything out of the ordinary, though I look for it everywhere,” said Vronsky, smiling.
“Very well, next Saturday,” answered Countess Nordston. “But you, Konstantin Dmitrich, do you believe in it?” she asked Levin.
“Why do you ask me? You know what I shall say.”
“But I want to hear your opinion.”

“My opinion is only this,” answered Levin: “that these turning tables prove that so-called educated society is no higher than the peasants. They believe in the evil eye, and in spells, and in love potions, and we…”
“So you don’t believe in it?”
“I can’t believe in it, Countess.”
“But if I have seen it myself?”
“Peasant women, too, tell how they have seen house-spirits with their own eyes.”
“So you think I am telling an untruth?”
And she laughed joylessly.

“Oh no, Masha, Konstantin Dmitrich says that he cannot believe it,” said Kitty, blushing for Levin; and Levin understood this and, still more irritated, wanted to answer; but Vronsky, with his open, cheerful smile, at once came to the rescue of a conversation that threatened to become unpleasant.
“You don’t admit the possibility at all?” he asked. “Why, we admit the existence of electricity, which we don’t understand; why can’t there be a new force, still unknown to us, which…”

“When electricity was found,” Levin interrupted quickly, “only the phenomenon had been discovered, and it was not known where it came from or what it produced, and centuries passed before anyone thought of applying it. The spiritualists, on the contrary, began with little tables writing for them and spirits coming to them, and only afterwards began to say that it was an unknown force.”
Vronsky listened attentively to Levin, as he always listened, evidently interested in his words.

“Yes, but the spiritualists say: we don’t know now what this force is, but the force exists, and here are the conditions under which it acts. Let the scientists work out what the force consists of. No, I don’t see why it can’t be a new force, if it…”
“Because,” Levin interrupted again, “with electricity, every time you rub resin on wool, a known phenomenon appears; and here it doesn’t every time; so it is not a natural phenomenon.”
Probably feeling that the conversation was taking a turn too serious for a drawing-room, Vronsky did not object but, trying to change the subject, smiled cheerfully and turned to the ladies.
“Let’s try it now, Countess,” he began; but Levin wanted to finish saying what he thought.

“I think,” he went on, “that this attempt of the spiritualists to explain their wonders by some new force is the least successful of all. They speak outright of a spiritual force and want to subject it to material experiment.”
Everyone was waiting for him to finish, and he felt it.
“And I think you would make an excellent medium,” said Countess Nordston; “there is something rapturous in you.”
Levin opened his mouth, wanted to say something, blushed, and said nothing.
“Let us try the tables now, Princess, please,” said Vronsky. “Princess, you will allow it?”
And Vronsky got up, looking about for a little table.

Kitty got up to go to the table and, as she passed, met Levin’s eyes. She pitied him with all her soul, all the more because she pitied him for an unhappiness of which she herself was the cause. “If I can be forgiven, forgive me,” her look said; “I am so happy.”

“I hate everyone, and you, and myself,” his look answered, and he took up his hat. But it was not his fate to leave. Just as they were about to settle round the table, and Levin to go, the old prince came in and, after greeting the ladies, turned to Levin.
“Ah!” he began joyfully. “Have you been here long? I didn’t even know you were here. Very glad to see you.”

The old prince sometimes said “thou” to Levin and sometimes “you”. He embraced Levin and, talking to him, did not notice Vronsky, who had stood up and was calmly waiting for the prince to turn to him.

Kitty felt how heavy her father’s kindness was for Levin after what had happened. She saw too how coldly her father at last answered Vronsky’s bow, and how Vronsky looked at her father with friendly bewilderment, trying to understand, and not understanding, how and why anyone could be unfriendly towards him; and she blushed.
“Prince, let us have Konstantin Dmitrich,” said Countess Nordston. “We want to make an experiment.”

“What experiment? Turning tables? Well, excuse me, ladies and gentlemen, but in my opinion it’s more fun to play hunt-the-ring,” said the old prince, looking at Vronsky and guessing that he had started it. “There is some sense in hunt-the-ring.”
Vronsky looked at the prince in surprise with his steady eyes and, smiling slightly, at once began talking to Countess Nordston about the big ball to be held the following week.
“I hope you will be there?” he said, turning to Kitty.

As soon as the old prince turned away from him, Levin went out unnoticed, and the last impression he carried away from that evening was Kitty’s smiling, happy face as she answered Vronsky’s question about the ball.
## Chapter XV

When the evening was over, Kitty told her mother about her conversation with Levin, and, in spite of all the pity she felt for Levin, the thought that she had received a proposal made her glad. She had no doubt that she had acted as she ought. But in bed she could not get to sleep for a long time. One impression pursued her relentlessly. It was Levin’s face, with his brows drawn together and his kind eyes looking out from under them in gloomy dejection, as he stood listening to her father and glancing at her and at Vronsky. And she felt so sorry for him that tears came into her eyes. But at once she thought of the man for whom she had given him up. She vividly remembered that manly, firm face, that noble calm, and the kindness to everyone that shone in everything; she remembered the love for her of the man she loved, and again her heart was glad, and she lay back on the pillow with a smile of happiness. “It’s a pity, a pity; but what can I do? It is not my fault,” she said to herself; but an inner voice told her something else. Whether she repented of having led Levin on, or of having refused him, she did not know. But her happiness was poisoned by doubts. “Lord have mercy, Lord have mercy, Lord have mercy!” she said to herself, until she fell asleep.
Meanwhile, downstairs, in the prince’s little study, one of those scenes was taking place that so often recur between parents over a favourite daughter.

“What? I’ll tell you what!” shouted the prince, waving his arms and at once wrapping his squirrel-lined dressing-gown round him again. “That you have no pride, no dignity, that you are disgracing, ruining our daughter with this matchmaking, this mean, idiotic matchmaking!”
“But, for the love of God, Prince, what have I done?” said the princess, almost in tears.

Happy and pleased after her talk with her daughter, she had come to the prince to say good night as usual, and, though she had not meant to tell him about Levin’s proposal and Kitty’s refusal, she had hinted to her husband that the business with Vronsky seemed to her quite settled, that it would be decided as soon as his mother arrived. And it was then, at these words, that the prince suddenly flared up and began shouting unseemly words.

“What have you done? This is what: first, you are luring a suitor, and all Moscow will talk, and rightly. If you give evening parties, invite everybody, not chosen little suitors. Invite all those young puppies” (so the prince called the young men of Moscow), “hire a pianist, and let them dance; not the way it was tonight, little suitors, and throwing them together. It disgusts me to see it, disgusts me; and you have got what you wanted, you have turned the girl’s head. Levin is a thousand times the better man. And as for that Petersburg dandy, they’re made by machine, they’re all cut to one pattern, and all trash. And even if he were a prince of the blood, my daughter has no need of anyone.”
“But what have I done?”
“Why, this…” the prince cried angrily.
“I know that if one listened to you,” the princess interrupted, “we should never marry our daughter at all. In that case we had better go off to the country.”
“And better we should.”
“But wait. Am I currying favour? I am not currying favour in the least. But a young man, and a very nice one, has fallen in love, and she, it seems…”

“Yes, it seems to you! And what if she really does fall in love, and he no more thinks of marrying than I do?… Oh! I wish my eyes had never seen it!… ‘Ah, spiritualism, ah, Nice, ah, at the ball…’” And the prince, imagining that he was imitating his wife, bobbed a curtsey at every word. “And when we have made Katenka unhappy, when she really takes it into her head…”
“But why do you think so?”

“I don’t think it, I know it; we have eyes for these things, not you women. I see a man who has serious intentions, and that’s Levin; and I see a peacock, like this featherhead, who only wants to amuse himself.”
“Well, once you take a thing into your head…”
“You’ll remember, but too late, as with Dashenka.”
“Well, all right, all right, let’s not talk about it,” the princess stopped him, remembering unhappy Dolly.
“Very well, and good night!”
And, making the sign of the cross over each other and kissing, but feeling that each remained of the same opinion, husband and wife parted.

At first the princess had been firmly convinced that this evening had decided Kitty’s fate and that there could be no doubt of Vronsky’s intentions; but her husband’s words troubled her. And, going back to her room, she too, just like Kitty, in terror before the unknown future, repeated several times in her heart: “Lord have mercy, Lord have mercy, Lord have mercy!”
## Chapter XVI

Vronsky had never known family life. His mother had been, in her youth, a brilliant society woman, who during her marriage, and especially afterwards, had many love affairs known to the whole of society. His father he barely remembered, and he had been brought up in the Corps of Pages.

Leaving school very young, a brilliant officer, he at once fell into the rut of the rich Petersburg military. Though he went now and then into Petersburg society, all his love interests lay outside it.

In Moscow, for the first time, after the luxurious and coarse life of Petersburg, he experienced the charm of intimacy with a sweet and innocent girl of good society, who fell in love with him. It never even entered his head that there could be anything wrong in his relations with Kitty. At balls he danced chiefly with her; he visited the house. He talked to her about what people usually talk about in society, all sorts of nonsense, but nonsense to which he could not help giving a special meaning for her. Although he said nothing to her that he could not have said in front of everyone, he felt that she was becoming more and more dependent on him; and the more he felt it, the more pleasant it was to him, and the more tender his feeling for her became. He did not know that his behaviour towards Kitty had a definite name, that it was luring a girl on without any intention of marrying her, and that such luring is one of the bad actions common among brilliant young men like himself. It seemed to him that he was the first to discover this pleasure, and he enjoyed his discovery.

If he could have heard what her parents were saying that evening, if he could have put himself at the family’s point of view and learned that Kitty would be unhappy if he did not marry her, he would have been very much surprised and would not have believed it. He could not believe that what gave such great and good pleasure to him, and above all to her, could be wrong. Still less could he have believed that he ought to marry.

Marriage had never presented itself to him as a possibility. Not only did he dislike family life, but in a family, and especially in a husband, in accordance with the general view of the bachelor world in which he lived, he saw something alien, hostile, and above all ridiculous. But although Vronsky had no suspicion of what her parents were saying, on leaving the Shcherbatskys’ that evening he felt that the secret spiritual bond that existed between him and Kitty had been strengthened so much that evening that something must be done. But what could and what should be done, he could not think.

“That is what is so delightful,” he thought, as he went home from the Shcherbatskys’, carrying away from them, as always, a pleasant feeling of purity and freshness, which came partly from his not having smoked the whole evening, and with it a new feeling of tenderness at her love for him, “that is what is so delightful, that nothing has been said, either by me or by her, but we understood each other so well in that invisible conversation of looks and tones that today, more clearly than ever, she has told me that she loves me. And how sweetly, simply and, above all, trustingly! I feel better myself, purer. I feel that I have a heart, and that there is a great deal of good in me. Those sweet, loving eyes! When she said: and very much…”
“Well, what of it? Why, nothing. It is good for me, and good for her.” And he began to think where he should finish the evening.

He went over in his imagination the places where he might go. “The club? A game of bezique, champagne with Ignatov? No, I won’t go. The Château des Fleurs; I’ll find Oblonsky there, songs, cancan? No, I’m tired of it. That is just why I love the Shcherbatskys, that I become better myself. I’ll go home.” He went straight to his rooms at Dussot’s hotel, ordered supper, and then, undressing, hardly had time to lay his head on the pillow before he fell into a sound and peaceful sleep, as always.
## Chapter XVII

The next day, at eleven in the morning, Vronsky drove to the station of the Petersburg railway to meet his mother, and the first person he came upon on the steps of the great staircase was Oblonsky, who was expecting his sister by the same train.
“Ah! Your excellency!” cried Oblonsky. “Whom are you meeting?”
“My mother,” answered Vronsky, smiling, as everyone did who met Oblonsky, and shaking his hand, and he went up the stairs with him. “She is due from Petersburg today.”
“And I waited for you till two o’clock. Where did you go after the Shcherbatskys’?”
“Home,” answered Vronsky. “I must confess, I felt so pleasant yesterday after the Shcherbatskys’ that I didn’t want to go anywhere.”
“‘I know a mettled horse by the brand upon his hide, and a youth in love I know by the look in his eyes,’” declaimed Stepan Arkadyich, exactly as he had to Levin before.
Vronsky smiled with an air that said he did not deny it, but at once changed the subject.
“And whom are you meeting?” he asked.
“I? A pretty woman,” said Oblonsky.
“You don’t say!”
“Honi soit qui mal y pense! My sister Anna.”
“Ah, Madame Karenina?” said Vronsky.
“You know her, I expect?”
“I think I do. Or no… Really, I don’t remember,” Vronsky answered absent-mindedly, vaguely picturing to himself at the name Karenina something stiff and dull.
“But Alexei Alexandrovich, my famous brother-in-law, you surely know. The whole world knows him.”
“That is, I know him by reputation and by sight. I know that he is clever, learned, something devout… But you know, that is not my… not in my line,” said Vronsky.
“Yes, he is a very remarkable man; a bit of a conservative, but a splendid man,” observed Stepan Arkadyich, “a splendid man.”
“Well, so much the better for him,” said Vronsky, smiling. “Ah, you’re here,” he said, turning to his mother’s tall old footman, who was standing by the door. “Come in here.”
Lately Vronsky, besides the pleasantness that Stepan Arkadyich had for everyone, had felt attached to him also because in his imagination he was connected with Kitty.
“Well, shall we give a supper for the diva on Sunday?” he said to him, taking his arm with a smile.
“Certainly. I’ll get up a subscription. Ah, did you meet my friend Levin yesterday?” asked Stepan Arkadyich.
“Of course. But he left rather soon.”
“He is a splendid fellow,” Oblonsky went on. “Isn’t he?”

“I don’t know,” answered Vronsky, “why it is that in all Muscovites, excepting, of course, those I am talking to,” he put in jokingly, “there is something sharp. They keep rearing up, getting angry, as though they all wanted to make you feel something…”
“There is that, it’s true, there is…” said Stepan Arkadyich, laughing merrily.
“Will it be long?” said Vronsky, turning to an attendant.
“The train has left the last station,” answered the man.

The approach of the train was more and more marked by the stir of preparations at the station, the running of porters, the appearance of gendarmes and attendants, and the arrival of people coming to meet it. Through the frosty steam one could see workmen in short sheepskin coats and soft felt boots crossing the rails of the curving lines. One could hear the whistle of an engine on the distant rails and the shifting of something heavy.

“No,” said Stepan Arkadyich, who very much wanted to tell Vronsky about Levin’s intentions towards Kitty. “No, you have not judged my Levin rightly. He is a very nervous man, and can be unpleasant, it’s true; but then sometimes he can be very nice. His is such an honest, truthful nature, and a heart of gold. But yesterday there were special reasons,” Stepan Arkadyich went on with a significant smile, quite forgetting the sincere sympathy he had felt for his friend the day before, and now feeling the same sympathy, only for Vronsky. “Yes, there was a reason why he might be either especially happy or especially unhappy.”
Vronsky stopped and asked directly:
“Meaning what? Or did he propose to your belle-sœur yesterday?…”

“Perhaps,” said Stepan Arkadyich. “Something of the sort struck me yesterday. And if he left early and was out of sorts as well, then it’s so… He has been in love so long, and I am very sorry for him.”

“So that’s it!… I think, though, that she can count on a better match,” said Vronsky, and, straightening his chest, he began walking again. “However, I don’t know him,” he added. “Yes, it’s a painful position! That is why most men prefer to have to do with Claras. There, failure only proves that you didn’t have enough money; but here your dignity is on the scales. But here is the train.”

And indeed the engine was already whistling in the distance. A few minutes later the platform trembled, and, puffing steam that the frost beat down to the ground, the engine rolled in, with the lever of its middle wheel slowly and rhythmically bending and stretching, and with the engine-driver, muffled up and covered in frost, bowing as it moved; and behind the tender, more and more slowly and shaking the platform more and more, came the luggage van with a dog whining in it; and at last, quivering before they stopped, the passenger carriages drew in.

A dashing guard, blowing his whistle as he went, jumped off, and after him the impatient passengers began getting down one by one: an officer of the Guards, holding himself straight and looking sternly about him; a fidgety little merchant with a bag, smiling cheerfully; a peasant with a sack over his shoulder.

Vronsky, standing beside Oblonsky, looked at the carriages and the people coming out, and quite forgot his mother. What he had just learned about Kitty excited and delighted him. His chest straightened in spite of him, and his eyes shone. He felt himself a conqueror.
“Countess Vronskaya is in this compartment,” said the dashing guard, coming up to Vronsky.

The guard’s words woke him and made him remember his mother and the meeting with her that lay ahead. In his soul he did not respect his mother and, without admitting it to himself, did not love her; though, by the notions of the circle he lived in, and by his upbringing, he could not imagine any relation to his mother other than one in the highest degree submissive and respectful, and the more outwardly submissive and respectful, the less he respected and loved her in his soul.
## Chapter XVIII

Vronsky followed the guard to the carriage and, at the entrance to the compartment, stopped to make way for a lady who was coming out. With the practised tact of a man of the world, from one glance at this lady’s appearance Vronsky placed her as belonging to the highest society. He begged her pardon and was going on into the carriage, but felt a need to look at her once more: not because she was very beautiful, nor because of the elegance and modest grace that could be seen in her whole figure, but because in the expression of her charming face, as she passed him, there was something especially warm and tender. When he looked round, she too turned her head. Her shining grey eyes, which seemed dark because of their thick lashes, rested in a friendly, attentive way on his face, as if she recognized him, and at once moved to the approaching crowd, as though looking for someone. In that short glance Vronsky had time to notice the restrained animation that played in her face and flitted between her shining eyes and the barely perceptible smile that curved her red lips. It was as though an excess of something so filled her whole being that it showed itself against her will, now in the brightness of her glance, now in her smile. She deliberately put out the light in her eyes, but it shone against her will in the barely perceptible smile.

Vronsky went into the carriage. His mother, a dry old lady with black eyes and ringlets, screwed up her eyes, peering at her son, and smiled slightly with her thin lips. Getting up from the little seat and handing her bag to her maid, she gave her son her small, dry hand and, raising his head from it, kissed him on the face.
“You got my telegram? You’re well? Thank God.”
“Did you have a good journey?” said her son, sitting down beside her and involuntarily listening to a woman’s voice outside the door. He knew it was the voice of the lady he had met at the entrance.
“All the same, I don’t agree with you,” the lady’s voice was saying.
“That’s the Petersburg view, madam.”
“Not the Petersburg view, simply a woman’s,” she answered.
“Well, allow me to kiss your hand.”
“Goodbye, Ivan Petrovich. And do look and see whether my brother is here, and send him to me,” said the lady at the very door, and she came back into the compartment.
“Well, have you found your brother?” said Countess Vronskaya, turning to the lady.
Vronsky remembered now that this was Madame Karenina.
“Your brother is here,” he said, getting up. “Forgive me, I didn’t recognize you; and our acquaintance was so short,” said Vronsky, bowing, “that you surely don’t remember me.”

“Oh, no,” she said, “I would have known you, because your mother and I, I believe, talked of nothing but you the whole way,” she said, allowing at last the animation that was asking to come out to show itself in a smile. “And still my brother isn’t here.”
“Do call him, Alyosha,” said the old countess.
Vronsky went out onto the platform and shouted:
“Oblonsky! Here!”

But Madame Karenina did not wait for her brother; seeing him, she stepped out of the carriage with a light, decided step. And as soon as her brother came up to her, with a movement that struck Vronsky by its decision and grace, she threw her left arm round her brother’s neck, drew him quickly to her and kissed him warmly. Vronsky, not taking his eyes off her, watched and smiled, without knowing why himself. But, remembering that his mother was waiting for him, he went back into the carriage.

“She’s very sweet, isn’t she?” said the countess of Madame Karenina. “Her husband put her in with me, and I was very glad. We talked the whole way. Well, and you, they say… vous filez le parfait amour. Tant mieux, mon cher, tant mieux.”
“I don’t know what you are hinting at, maman,” her son answered coldly. “Well, maman, let us go.”
Madame Karenina came into the carriage again to say goodbye to the countess.
“Well, Countess, you have met your son, and I my brother,” she said gaily. “And all my stories were exhausted; I should have had nothing more to tell.”

“Oh no, my dear,” said the countess, taking her hand, “I could go round the world with you and not be bored. You are one of those sweet women with whom it is pleasant both to talk and to be silent. And please don’t think about your son: one can’t never be parted.”
Madame Karenina stood motionless, holding herself extremely straight, and her eyes were smiling.
“Anna Arkadyevna,” said the countess, explaining to her son, “has a little son of eight, I believe, and she has never been parted from him, and she keeps tormenting herself for having left him.”
“Yes, the countess and I talked all the time, I about my son and she about hers,” said Madame Karenina, and again a smile lit up her face, a warm smile meant for him.

“That must have bored you very much,” he said, catching at once, on the wing, this ball of coquetry that she had thrown him. But she evidently did not want to go on talking in that tone, and she turned to the old countess.
“Thank you so much. I hardly noticed how I spent yesterday. Goodbye, Countess.”
“Goodbye, my dear,” answered the countess. “Let me kiss your pretty little face. I’ll say it straight out, simply, like an old woman: I have grown fond of you.”

Stock phrase as it was, Madame Karenina evidently believed it from her heart and was glad of it. She blushed, bent down slightly, offered her face to the countess’s lips, straightened up again and, with the same smile hovering between her lips and her eyes, gave her hand to Vronsky. He pressed the little hand she gave him and was glad, as of something special, of the energetic pressure with which she firmly and boldly shook his hand. She went out with a quick step that carried her rather full body so strangely lightly.
“Very sweet,” said the old lady.

Her son was thinking the same. He followed her with his eyes until her graceful figure disappeared, and the smile stayed on his face. Through the window he saw her go up to her brother, put her hand on his arm and begin telling him something animatedly, evidently about something that had nothing to do with him, Vronsky; and this seemed to him annoying.
“Well, maman, you are perfectly well?” he repeated, turning to his mother.
“Everything is fine, splendid. Alexandre was very sweet. And Marie has grown very pretty. She is very interesting.”
And again she began telling what interested her most, about the christening of her grandson, for which she had gone to Petersburg, and about the Emperor’s special favour to her elder son.
“Here is Lavrenty,” said Vronsky, looking out of the window. “Now let us go, if you like.”
The old butler who was travelling with the countess appeared in the carriage to say that everything was ready, and the countess got up to go.
“Come along, there are few people now,” said Vronsky.

The maid took the bag and the little dog, the butler and a porter the other bags. Vronsky gave his mother his arm; but just as they were coming out of the carriage, several people with frightened faces suddenly ran past. The station-master ran past too, in his cap of an unusual colour. Evidently something unusual had happened. People were running back from the train.
“What?… What?… Where?… Threw himself!… Crushed!…” could be heard among the passers-by.
Stepan Arkadyich, with his sister on his arm, came back, with frightened faces too, and stopped at the entrance to the carriage, avoiding the crowd.
The ladies went into the carriage, while Vronsky and Stepan Arkadyich followed the crowd to find out the details of the accident.
A watchman, whether he was drunk or too muffled up against the hard frost, had not heard a train being shunted backwards, and he had been crushed.
Even before Vronsky and Oblonsky came back, the ladies had learned these details from the butler.
Oblonsky and Vronsky had both seen the mangled body. Oblonsky was evidently suffering. He was wincing and seemed ready to cry.
“Ah, how horrible! Ah, Anna, if you had seen it! Ah, how horrible!” he kept saying.
Vronsky was silent, and his handsome face was serious but perfectly calm.

“Ah, if you had seen it, Countess,” said Stepan Arkadyich. “And his wife was there… It was dreadful to see her… She threw herself on the body. They say he alone supported an enormous family. How horrible!”
“Can’t something be done for her?” said Madame Karenina in an agitated whisper.
Vronsky looked at her and at once went out of the carriage.
“I’ll be back directly, maman,” he added, turning round in the doorway.
When he came back a few minutes later, Stepan Arkadyich was already talking to the countess about the new singer, and the countess was looking impatiently towards the door, waiting for her son.

“Now let us go,” said Vronsky, coming in. They went out together. Vronsky walked in front with his mother. Behind came Madame Karenina with her brother. At the exit the station-master, who had overtaken him, came up to Vronsky.
“You gave my assistant two hundred roubles. Would you kindly say whom you intend them for?”
“For the widow,” said Vronsky, shrugging his shoulders. “I don’t see what there is to ask.”
“You gave that?” Oblonsky called out behind him, and, pressing his sister’s arm, he added: “Very nice, very nice! Isn’t he a splendid fellow? My respects, Countess.”
And he and his sister stopped, looking for her maid.
When they came out, the Vronskys’ carriage had already driven off. The people coming out were still talking about what had happened.
“What a horrible death!” said some gentleman, passing by. “They say he was cut in two.”
“On the contrary, I think it’s the easiest, it’s instantaneous,” observed another.
“How is it they don’t take measures?” said a third.
Madame Karenina got into the carriage, and Stepan Arkadyich saw with surprise that her lips were trembling and that she could hardly hold back her tears.
“What is the matter, Anna?” he asked, when they had driven a few hundred yards.
“It is a bad omen,” she said.
“What nonsense!” said Stepan Arkadyich. “You have come, that’s the main thing. You can’t imagine how much I am counting on you.”
“And have you known Vronsky long?” she asked.
“Yes. You know, we are hoping he will marry Kitty.”

“Yes?” said Anna quietly. “Well, now let us talk about you,” she added, shaking her head as if she wanted physically to drive away something superfluous that was in her way. “Let us talk about your affairs. I got your letter, and here I am.”
“Yes, all my hope is in you,” said Stepan Arkadyich.
“Well, tell me everything.”
And Stepan Arkadyich began to tell her.
When they reached the house, Oblonsky helped his sister out, sighed, pressed her hand, and drove off to his office.
## Part One · Chapter XIX

When Anna came into the room, Dolly was sitting in the little drawing-room with a plump, white-headed little boy, who already looked like his father, and was hearing his lesson in French reading. The boy was reading, twisting in his hand a button of his jacket that was barely holding on and trying to tear it off. Several times his mother took his hand away, but the plump little hand took hold of the button again. His mother tore off the button and put it in her pocket.

“Keep your hands still, Grisha,” she said, and took up her blanket again, a piece of work she had had on hand for a long time, which she always took up in hard moments; she was knitting it now nervously, flicking the yarn over with her finger and counting the stitches. Although she had sent word to her husband the day before that it was nothing to her whether his sister came or not, she had got everything ready for her arrival and was waiting for her sister-in-law with agitation.

Dolly was crushed by her grief, entirely swallowed up in it. Still, she remembered that Anna, her sister-in-law, was the wife of one of the most important persons in Petersburg, and a Petersburg grande dame. And thanks to this circumstance she had not done what she had told her husband, that is, she had not forgotten that her sister-in-law was coming. “And, after all, Anna is not to blame for anything,” thought Dolly. “I know nothing of her but what is very good, and towards me I have seen nothing from her but kindness and friendship.” True, as far as she could remember her impression of the Karenins’ house in Petersburg, she had not liked the house itself; there was something false in the whole pattern of their family life. “But why should I not receive her? If only she doesn’t take it into her head to console me!” thought Dolly. “All the consolations and exhortations and Christian forgiveness, I have thought it all over a thousand times already, and none of it is any use.”

All these days Dolly had been alone with the children. She did not want to talk about her grief, and with that grief in her soul she could not talk about anything else. She knew that one way or another she would pour everything out to Anna; and now she was glad at the thought of how she would pour it out, now angry at the necessity of talking about her humiliation with her, his sister, and of hearing from her ready-made phrases of exhortation and consolation.
As often happens, she had been watching the clock and expecting her every minute, and missed exactly the minute when the visitor arrived, so that she did not hear the bell.

Hearing the rustle of a dress and light steps already at the door, she looked round, and her tormented face expressed in spite of herself not joy but surprise. She got up and embraced her sister-in-law.
“What, here already?” she said, kissing her.
“Dolly, how glad I am to see you!”

“And I am glad,” said Dolly, smiling faintly and trying to tell from the expression of Anna’s face whether she knew. “She must know,” she thought, noticing the sympathy in Anna’s face. “Well, come, I’ll take you to your room,” she went on, trying to put off as long as possible the moment of explanation.
“Is this Grisha? My goodness, how he has grown!” said Anna, and, kissing him, without taking her eyes off Dolly, she stopped and blushed. “No, let us not go anywhere.”
She took off her scarf and her hat, and, catching it in a lock of her black hair, which curled everywhere, she shook her head to free it.
“And you are radiant with happiness and health!” said Dolly, almost with envy.

“I?… Yes,” said Anna. “Goodness, Tanya! The same age as my Seryozha,” she added, turning to the little girl, who had run in. She took her in her arms and kissed her. “A lovely little girl, lovely! Show me all of them.”
She named them, and remembered not only the names but the years, the months, the characters and the illnesses of all the children, and Dolly could not help appreciating it.
“Well then, let us go to them,” she said. “It’s a pity Vasya is asleep now.”
When they had seen the children, they sat down, alone now, in the drawing-room over coffee. Anna took hold of the tray and then pushed it away.
“Dolly,” she said, “he has told me.”
Dolly looked coldly at Anna. She was waiting now for phrases of pretended sympathy; but Anna said nothing of the kind.
“Dolly, darling!” she said. “I don’t want to speak to you for him, or to console you; that’s impossible. But, my dear, I am simply sorry, sorry for you with all my heart!”

From under the thick lashes of her shining eyes tears suddenly appeared. She moved closer to her sister-in-law and took her hand in her own energetic little hand. Dolly did not draw away, but her face did not change its dry expression. She said:
“There is no consoling me. Everything is lost after what has happened, everything is gone!”
And as soon as she had said this, the expression of her face suddenly softened. Anna lifted Dolly’s dry, thin hand, kissed it and said:
“But, Dolly, what is to be done, what is to be done? How is it best to act in this terrible situation? That is what we must think about.”

“Everything is over, and that’s all,” said Dolly. “And the worst of it, you understand, is that I can’t leave him; there are the children, I am tied. And I can’t live with him; it is torture to me to see him.”
“Dolly, darling, he has told me, but I want to hear it from you; tell me everything.”
Dolly looked at her questioningly. Unfeigned sympathy and love could be seen in Anna’s face.

“Very well,” she said suddenly. “But I shall tell it from the beginning. You know how I married. With maman’s upbringing I was not only innocent, I was stupid. I knew nothing. They say, I know, that husbands tell their wives about their former lives, but Stiva…” She corrected herself. “Stepan Arkadyich told me nothing. You won’t believe it, but until now I thought I was the only woman he had known. That is how I lived for eight years. You must understand that not only did I not suspect unfaithfulness, I thought it impossible; and then, imagine, with such ideas, suddenly to learn all the horror, all the vileness… You must understand me. To be completely sure of one’s happiness, and suddenly…” Dolly went on, holding back her sobs, “and to receive a letter… his letter to his mistress, to my governess. No, it is too horrible!” She hurriedly took out her handkerchief and covered her face with it. “I could understand being carried away,” she went on, after a silence, “but to deceive me deliberately, cunningly… and with whom?… To go on being my husband together with her… it is horrible! You can’t understand…”
“Oh no, I do understand! I understand, dear Dolly, I understand,” said Anna, pressing her hand.
“And do you think he understands all the horror of my position?” Dolly went on. “Not in the least! He is happy and contented.”
“Oh, no!” Anna interrupted quickly. “He is pitiful, he is crushed with remorse…”
“Is he capable of remorse?” Dolly interrupted, peering attentively into her sister-in-law’s face.

“Yes, I know him. I could not look at him without pity. We both know him. He is kind, but he is proud, and now he is so humiliated. What touched me most” (and here Anna guessed the main thing that could touch Dolly) “is that two things torment him: that he is ashamed before the children, and that he, loving you… yes, yes, loving you more than anything in the world,” she hurriedly interrupted Dolly, who wanted to object, “has hurt you, has struck you down. ‘No, no, she will not forgive,’ he keeps saying.”
Dolly looked thoughtfully past her sister-in-law as she listened to her words.

“Yes, I understand that his position is terrible; it is worse for the guilty one than for the innocent,” she said, “if he feels that all the unhappiness comes from his guilt. But how can I forgive, how can I be his wife again after her? To live with him now will be torture to me, precisely because I loved him as I did, because I love my past love for him…”
And sobs cut off her words.
But, as though on purpose, every time she softened she began talking again of what exasperated her.

“She is young, you know, she is pretty,” she went on. “Do you understand, Anna, who has taken my youth and my beauty? He and his children. I have served my time with him, and everything that was mine has gone in that service, and now of course a fresh, vulgar creature is more pleasing to him. They must have talked about me together, or, worse still, kept silent about me, do you understand?” Again her eyes kindled with hatred. “And after that he will tell me… What, shall I believe him? Never. No, everything is finished, everything that was a comfort, the reward of work, of suffering… Would you believe it? I was teaching Grisha just now: it used to be a joy, and now it is torture.
