Why do I try, why do I toil? What are the children for? The terrible thing is that suddenly my soul has turned over, and instead of love and tenderness I have nothing but anger for him, yes, anger. I could kill him and…”
“Darling, Dolly, I understand, but don’t torment yourself. You are so hurt, so worked up, that you see many things wrongly.”
Dolly grew quiet, and for two minutes or so they were silent.
“What is to be done? Think, Anna, help me. I have thought everything over and I see nothing.”
Anna could think of nothing, but her heart responded directly to every word, to every expression of her sister-in-law’s face.

“I will say one thing,” Anna began. “I am his sister, I know his character, this capacity of forgetting everything, everything” (she made a gesture in front of her forehead), “this capacity of being completely carried away, but then also of complete repentance. He doesn’t believe, he doesn’t understand now, how he could have done what he did.”
“No, he understands, he understood!” Dolly interrupted. “But I… you forget me… is it any easier for me?”

“Wait! When he talked to me, I confess I did not yet understand all the horror of your position. I saw only him, and that the family was in disorder; I was sorry for him; but now that I have talked with you, I, as a woman, see something else; I see your suffering, and I can’t tell you how sorry I am for you! But, Dolly darling, I understand your suffering completely; only one thing I don’t know: I don’t know… I don’t know how much love there still is for him in your soul. That you know: whether there is enough to make forgiveness possible. If there is, then forgive!”
“No,” Dolly began; but Anna interrupted her, kissing her hand once more.

“I know the world better than you,” she said. “I know these men, like Stiva, how they look at these things. You say that he talked to her about you. That never happened. These men are unfaithful, but their own hearth and their wife are sacred to them. Somehow with them these women remain in contempt and don’t interfere with the family. They draw some line that can’t be crossed between the family and that. I don’t understand it, but that is how it is.”
“Yes, but he kissed her…”

“Dolly, wait, darling. I saw Stiva when he was in love with you. I remember that time, when he came to me and cried as he talked about you, and what poetry and what a height you were for him; and I know that the longer he lived with you, the higher you became for him. Why, we used to laugh at him because he added to every word: ‘Dolly is a wonderful woman.’ You always were and still are a divinity for him, and this infatuation was not of his soul…”
“But what if this infatuation happens again?”
“It can’t, as I understand it…”
“Yes, but would you forgive?”

“I don’t know. I can’t judge… Yes, I can,” said Anna, after thinking; and, grasping the situation in her mind and weighing it on her inner scales, she added: “Yes, I can, I can, I can. Yes, I would forgive. I would not be the same, no; but I would forgive, and forgive as though it had not happened, had not happened at all.”

“Well, of course,” Dolly broke in quickly, as though saying what she had thought more than once, “otherwise it would not be forgiveness. If one forgives, then completely, completely. Well, come, I’ll take you to your room,” she said, getting up; and on the way Dolly embraced Anna. “My dear, how glad I am you have come, how glad. I feel better, much better.”
## Chapter XX

All that day Anna spent at home, that is, at the Oblonskys’, and received no one, though some of her acquaintances, having already heard of her arrival, called that same day. Anna spent the whole morning with Dolly and the children. She only sent a little note to her brother, telling him he must dine at home. “Come; God is merciful,” she wrote.

Oblonsky dined at home; the conversation was general, and his wife talked to him and called him “thou”, which she had not done before. In the relations of husband and wife the same estrangement remained, but there was no longer any talk of separation, and Stepan Arkadyich saw the possibility of an explanation and a reconciliation.

Immediately after dinner Kitty came. She knew Anna Arkadyevna, but very little, and she was coming now to her sister’s not without some fear of how she would be received by this Petersburg society lady whom everyone praised so. But Anna Arkadyevna liked her; she saw that at once. Anna was evidently admiring her beauty and youth, and before Kitty knew where she was, she felt herself not only under her influence but in love with her, as young girls are capable of falling in love with married and older women. Anna was not like a society lady or the mother of a son of eight; she would rather have seemed a girl of twenty, by the suppleness of her movements, her freshness, and the animation settled in her face that broke out now in a smile, now in a glance, if it had not been for the serious, sometimes sad expression of her eyes, which struck Kitty and drew her. Kitty felt that Anna was perfectly simple and hid nothing, but that there was in her some other, higher world of interests, complex and poetic, out of Kitty’s reach.
After dinner, when Dolly had gone to her room, Anna got up quickly and went up to her brother, who was lighting a cigar.
“Stiva,” she said to him, winking gaily, making the sign of the cross over him and pointing to the door with her eyes. “Go, and God help you.”
He threw down the cigar, understanding her, and disappeared through the door.

When Stepan Arkadyich had gone, she went back to the sofa, where she had been sitting surrounded by the children. Whether because the children saw that mama loved this aunt, or because they themselves felt a special charm in her, the elder two, and the younger ones after them, as often happens with children, had attached themselves to the new aunt even before dinner and would not leave her. And something like a game had come about among them, which consisted in sitting as close to their aunt as possible, touching her, holding her little hand, kissing it, playing with her ring, or at least touching the flounce of her dress.
“Come, come, let us sit the way we were sitting before,” said Anna Arkadyevna, sitting down in her place.
And again Grisha pushed his head under her arm and leaned his head against her dress, and beamed with pride and happiness.
“So, when is the ball now?” she said, turning to Kitty.
“Next week, and a splendid ball. One of those balls where it is always gay.”
“And are there balls where it is always gay?” said Anna with tender mockery.
“It’s strange, but there are. At the Bobrishchevs’ it is always gay, and at the Nikitins’ too, but at the Mezhkovs’ it is always dull. Haven’t you noticed?”

“No, my dear, for me there are no longer any balls where it is gay,” said Anna, and Kitty saw in her eyes that special world which was not open to her. “For me there are some where it is less hard and dull…”
“How can you be bored at a ball?”
“Why can’t I be bored at a ball?” asked Anna.
Kitty noticed that Anna knew what answer would follow.
“Because you are always the best of all.”
Anna had the ability to blush. She blushed and said:
“In the first place, never; and in the second, even if it were so, what would it matter to me?”
“Will you go to this ball?” asked Kitty.
“I think it will be impossible not to. Here, take this,” she said to Tanya, who was pulling the ring, which came off easily, from her white finger, slender at the tip.
“I shall be very glad if you go. I should so like to see you at the ball.”

“At least, if I have to go, I shall comfort myself with the thought that it will give you pleasure… Grisha, don’t pull, please, it’s all coming down as it is,” she said, putting back a loose lock of hair that Grisha was playing with.
“I imagine you at the ball in lilac.”

“Why lilac, of all things?” asked Anna, smiling. “Well, children, run along, run along. Do you hear? Miss Hull is calling you to tea,” she said, tearing the children away from her and sending them to the dining-room.
“And I know why you want me at the ball. You expect a great deal from this ball, and you want everyone to be there, everyone to take part.”
“How do you know? Yes.”

“Oh, what a good time yours is,” Anna went on. “I remember and know that blue mist, like the mist on the mountains in Switzerland. That mist that covers everything in that blissful time when childhood is just about to end, and out of that vast circle, happy and gay, a path is made, narrower and narrower, and it is gay and frightening to go into that long suite of rooms, though it is bright and beautiful… Who has not been through that?”
Kitty smiled in silence. “But how did she go through it? How I should like to know her whole romance,” thought Kitty, remembering the unpoetic appearance of Alexei Alexandrovich, her husband.
“I know something. Stiva told me, and I congratulate you; I like him very much,” Anna went on. “I met Vronsky at the railway station.”
“Ah, was he there?” asked Kitty, blushing. “What did Stiva tell you?”

“Stiva blabbed everything to me. And I should be very glad. I travelled yesterday with Vronsky’s mother,” she went on, “and his mother talked to me about him without stopping; he is her favourite; I know how partial mothers are, but…”
“What did his mother tell you?”

“Oh, a great deal! And I know he is her favourite, but still one can see he is a knight… Well, for instance, she told me that he wanted to give his whole fortune to his brother, that when he was still a child he did something extraordinary, saved a woman from drowning. In a word, a hero,” said Anna, smiling and remembering the two hundred roubles he had given at the station.

But she did not tell about the two hundred roubles. For some reason it was unpleasant for her to remember it. She felt that there was something in it that concerned her, something that ought not to have been.

“She begged me very much to go and see her,” Anna went on, “and I shall be glad to see the old lady, and I shall go to her tomorrow. But, thank God, Stiva is staying a long time in Dolly’s room,” Anna added, changing the subject and getting up, displeased about something, as it seemed to Kitty.
“No, me first! No, me!” shouted the children, who had finished their tea, running out to Aunt Anna.
“All together!” said Anna, and, laughing, she ran to meet them, put her arms round them and tumbled over the whole heap of wriggling children, squealing with delight.
## Chapter XXI
Dolly came out of her room for the grown-ups’ tea. Stepan Arkadyich did not come out. He must have left his wife’s room by the back way.
“I am afraid you will be cold upstairs,” Dolly remarked, turning to Anna. “I want to move you downstairs, and we shall be nearer.”
“Oh, please don’t worry about me,” answered Anna, peering into Dolly’s face and trying to make out whether there had been a reconciliation or not.
“It will be lighter for you here,” answered her sister-in-law.
“I tell you, I sleep anywhere and always like a marmot.”
“What is all this?” said Stepan Arkadyich, coming out of the study and turning to his wife.
From his tone both Kitty and Anna understood at once that the reconciliation had taken place.
“I want to move Anna downstairs, but the curtains must be hung differently. No one will manage it; I must do it myself,” answered Dolly, turning to him.
“God knows whether they have been fully reconciled,” thought Anna, hearing her tone, cold and calm.
“Oh, come now, Dolly, you are always making difficulties,” said her husband. “Well, if you like, I’ll do it all…”
“Yes, they must have been reconciled,” thought Anna.

“I know how you will do it all,” answered Dolly. “You’ll tell Matvei to do what can’t be done, and go off yourself, and he will get it all muddled.” And the habitual mocking smile wrinkled the corners of Dolly’s lips as she said it.
“A full, full reconciliation, full,” thought Anna. “Thank God!” And, glad that she had been the cause of it, she went up to Dolly and kissed her.
“Not at all; why do you despise Matvei and me so?” said Stepan Arkadyich, smiling just perceptibly and turning to his wife.

All the evening Dolly, as always, was a little mocking towards her husband, and Stepan Arkadyich was contented and cheerful, but only so far as not to show that, being forgiven, he had forgotten his guilt.

At half past nine the especially joyful and pleasant evening family talk round the tea-table at the Oblonskys’ was broken by an event that was, to all appearances, the simplest, yet this simple event for some reason seemed strange to everyone. While they were talking about common acquaintances in Petersburg, Anna got up quickly.
“I have her in my album,” she said; “and by the way, I’ll show you my Seryozha,” she added with a proud mother’s smile.

Towards ten o’clock, when she usually said good night to her son, and often put him to bed herself before going to a ball, she felt sad at being so far from him; and whatever they talked about, she kept returning in her thoughts to her curly-headed Seryozha. She wanted to look at his photograph and talk about him. Seizing the first pretext, she got up and went for the album with her light, decided step. The stairs up to her room came out onto the landing of the big, warm front staircase.
Just as she was leaving the drawing-room, the bell rang in the hall.
“Who can that be?” said Dolly.
“It’s early to fetch me, and late for anyone else,” remarked Kitty.

“Papers, I expect,” added Stepan Arkadyich; and when Anna was passing the head of the staircase, a servant was running up to announce the visitor, and the visitor himself was standing by the lamp. Anna, glancing down, at once recognized Vronsky, and a strange feeling of pleasure and at the same time of fear of something suddenly stirred in her heart. He was standing without taking off his overcoat and getting something out of his pocket. At the moment when she reached the middle of the staircase he raised his eyes and saw her, and something ashamed and frightened came into the expression of his face. Bending her head slightly, she passed on, and after her could be heard Stepan Arkadyich’s loud voice calling him to come in, and the quiet, soft, calm voice of Vronsky refusing.

When Anna came back with the album he was no longer there, and Stepan Arkadyich was telling them that he had called to find out about the dinner they were giving the next day for a visiting celebrity.
“He wouldn’t come in for anything. He’s a strange fellow,” Stepan Arkadyich added.

Kitty blushed. She thought that she alone understood why he had come and why he had not come in. “He has been to our house,” she thought, “and didn’t find me, and thought I was here; but he didn’t come in because he thought it was late, and Anna is here.”
They all looked at one another without saying anything, and began looking at Anna’s album.

There was nothing either unusual or strange in a man calling on a friend at half past nine to find out the details of a dinner being planned, and not coming in; but it seemed strange to everyone. More than to anyone, it seemed strange and not right to Anna.
## Chapter XXII

The ball had only just begun when Kitty and her mother went up the great staircase, flooded with light and lined with flowers and with footmen in powder and red coats. From the rooms came a steady murmur of movement, as in a beehive, and while they were setting their hair right before a mirror on the landing among the trees, the carefully distinct sounds of the orchestra’s violins could be heard from the ballroom, beginning the first waltz. A little old man in civilian dress, who was setting his grey side-locks straight before another mirror and giving off a smell of scent, ran into them on the stairs and stood aside, evidently admiring Kitty, whom he did not know. A beardless youth, one of those society youths whom the old Prince Shcherbatsky called puppies, in an exceedingly low-cut waistcoat, straightening his white tie as he went, bowed to them, ran past, came back, and asked Kitty for the quadrille. The first quadrille had already been given to Vronsky; she had to give this youth the second. An officer, buttoning his glove, stood aside at the door, and, stroking his moustache, admired the rosy Kitty.

Although her dress, her hair and all the preparations for the ball had cost Kitty great trouble and thought, she now, in her elaborate tulle dress over a pink slip, entered the ball as freely and simply as if all these rosettes and laces, all the details of her toilette, had not cost her or her household a moment’s attention, as if she had been born in this tulle and lace, with this high coiffure and the rose and two leaves on top of it.

When the old princess, before they went into the ballroom, wanted to set straight the twisted ribbon of her sash, Kitty drew back slightly. She felt that everything on her must be right and graceful of itself, and that nothing needed setting straight.

Kitty was having one of her happy days. Her dress was not tight anywhere; the lace bertha did not slip down anywhere; the rosettes were not crushed or torn off; the pink slippers with their high curved heels did not pinch but gladdened her feet. The thick plaits of fair hair stayed on her little head as if they were her own. All three buttons had done up without tearing on the long glove that wrapped her arm without changing its shape. The black velvet ribbon of her locket encircled her neck with particular tenderness. This velvet ribbon was a delight, and at home, looking at her neck in the mirror, Kitty had felt that this velvet was speaking. About everything else there might still be some doubt, but the velvet was a delight. Kitty smiled here too at the ball, glancing at it in a mirror. In her bare shoulders and arms Kitty felt a cold, marble feeling, a sensation she especially loved. Her eyes shone, and her red lips could not help smiling from the awareness of her attractiveness. She had hardly entered the ballroom and reached the throng of ladies, all tulle, ribbons, lace and flowers, waiting to be asked to dance (Kitty never stood long in that throng), when she was already asked for a waltz, and asked by the best partner, the chief partner in the ballroom hierarchy, the famous director of balls, the master of ceremonies, a married, handsome and well-built man, Yegorushka Korsunsky. He had only just left Countess Banina, with whom he had danced the first round of the waltz, and, looking over his domain, that is, the few couples who had started dancing, he saw Kitty coming in and ran up to her with that special free-and-easy amble peculiar to directors of balls, and, bowing, without even asking whether she wished it, lifted his arm to put it round her slender waist. She looked round for someone to give her fan to, and the hostess, smiling at her, took it.
“How good of you to come in time,” he said, putting his arm round her waist. “What a habit people have of coming late.”
She laid her left hand, bent, on his shoulder, and her little feet in pink slippers moved quickly, lightly and evenly in time to the music over the slippery parquet.

“One rests, waltzing with you,” he said to her, setting off in the first unhurried steps of the waltz. “Delightful, such lightness, précision,” he said to her what he said to almost all his good acquaintances.

She smiled at his praise and went on looking about the room over his shoulder. She was not a girl coming out for the first time, for whom at a ball all the faces merge into one magical impression; nor was she a girl dragged around to balls, to whom all the faces of a ball are so familiar that they bore her; she was midway between these two: she was excited, and at the same time so much in possession of herself that she could observe. In the left corner of the room, she saw, the flower of society had gathered. There was Lidi, Korsunsky’s wife, a beauty bare beyond what was possible; there was the hostess; there Krivin’s bald head shone, he who was always where the flower of society was; the young men looked that way, not daring to go up; and there her eyes found Stiva, and then she saw Anna’s lovely figure and head in a black velvet dress. And he was there. Kitty had not seen him since the evening when she refused Levin. With her long-sighted eyes Kitty knew him at once, and even noticed that he was looking at her.
“Well, another round? You are not tired?” said Korsunsky, a little out of breath.
“No, thank you.”
“Where shall I take you?”
“Madame Karenina is here, I think… take me to her.”
“Wherever you wish.”

And Korsunsky waltzed, slackening his step, straight towards the throng in the left corner of the room, saying, “Pardon, mesdames, pardon, pardon, mesdames,” and, tacking through the sea of lace, tulle and ribbons without catching on a single feather, he turned his partner sharply, so that her slender legs in their openwork stockings were shown, and her train spread out like a fan and covered Krivin’s knees. Korsunsky bowed, straightened his open shirt-front and gave her his arm to take her to Anna Arkadyevna. Kitty, flushed, took her train off Krivin’s knees and, a little giddy, looked round, searching for Anna. Anna was standing surrounded by ladies and men, talking. Anna was not in lilac, as Kitty had so wanted, but in a black, low-cut velvet dress that showed her full shoulders and bosom, shaped as if from old ivory, and her rounded arms with their slender, tiny wrists. The whole dress was trimmed with Venetian lace. On her head, in her black hair, her own without any addition, was a little wreath of pansies, and another like it on the black ribbon of her sash among the white lace. Her coiffure was not noticeable. All that was noticeable, and that adorned her, were those wilful short ringlets of curly hair that always escaped at the nape of her neck and at her temples. On her finely shaped, strong neck was a string of pearls.

Kitty had seen Anna every day; she was in love with her, and had pictured her without fail in lilac. But now, seeing her in black, she felt that she had not understood all her charm. She now saw her as entirely new and unexpected. Now she understood that Anna could not have been in lilac, and that her charm lay precisely in this: that she always stood out from her dress, that her dress could never be seen on her. And the black dress with its rich lace could not be seen on her; it was only a frame, and only she could be seen, simple, natural, elegant, and at the same time gay and animated.
She was standing, as always, holding herself extremely straight, and, when Kitty came up to the group, she was talking to the master of the house, her head turned slightly towards him.

“No, I will not throw a stone,” she was answering him about something, “though I don’t understand it,” she went on, shrugging her shoulders; and at once, with a tender smile of patronage, she turned to Kitty. Glancing over her dress with a quick feminine look, she made a movement of her head, barely noticeable but understood by Kitty, approving her dress and her beauty. “You come into the ballroom dancing,” she added.

“This is one of my most faithful helpers,” said Korsunsky, bowing to Anna Arkadyevna, whom he had not yet seen. “The princess helps to make a ball gay and beautiful. Anna Arkadyevna, a round of the waltz,” he said, bending forward.
“Do you two know each other?” asked the host.
“Whom do we not know? My wife and I are like white wolves; everyone knows us,” answered Korsunsky. “A round of the waltz, Anna Arkadyevna.”
“I don’t dance when it is possible not to dance,” she said.
“But tonight it is impossible,” answered Korsunsky.
At that moment Vronsky came up.
“Well, if it is impossible not to dance tonight, then let us go,” she said, not noticing Vronsky’s bow, and quickly put her hand on Korsunsky’s shoulder.

“Why is she displeased with him?” thought Kitty, noticing that Anna had deliberately not answered Vronsky’s bow. Vronsky came up to Kitty, reminding her of the first quadrille and regretting that all this time he had not had the pleasure of seeing her. Kitty listened to him, looking admiringly at Anna waltzing. She was waiting for him to ask her to waltz, but he did not, and she looked at him in surprise. He blushed and hurriedly asked her to waltz; but no sooner had he put his arm round her slender waist and taken the first step than the music suddenly stopped. Kitty looked at his face, which was so near her; and long afterwards, for several years, that look full of love which she gave him then, and to which he did not answer, cut her heart with tormenting shame.
“Pardon, pardon! A waltz, a waltz!” Korsunsky shouted from the other side of the room, and, catching up the first young lady who came to hand, began dancing himself.
## Chapter XXIII

Vronsky and Kitty went round the room several times in the waltz. After the waltz Kitty went to her mother, and had hardly time to say a few words to Countess Nordston before Vronsky came for her for the first quadrille. Nothing significant was said during the quadrille; there was a broken conversation, now about the Korsunskys, husband and wife, whom he described very amusingly as sweet children of forty, now about the public theatre that was being planned; and only once did the conversation touch her to the quick, when he asked about Levin, whether he was here, and added that he had liked him very much. But Kitty had not expected more from the quadrille. She was waiting with a sinking heart for the mazurka. It seemed to her that in the mazurka everything must be decided. That he had not asked her for the mazurka during the quadrille did not trouble her. She was sure that she would dance the mazurka with him, as at earlier balls, and she had refused five men for the mazurka, saying that she was engaged. The whole ball, up to the last quadrille, was for Kitty a magic dream of joyful colours, sounds and movements. She did not dance only when she felt too tired and asked for a rest. But, dancing the last quadrille with one of the dull young men whom it was impossible to refuse, she happened to be vis-à-vis with Vronsky and Anna. She had not come near Anna since the beginning of the evening, and here suddenly she saw her again as entirely new and unexpected. She saw in her the feature so familiar to herself, of excitement at success. She saw that Anna was drunk with the wine of the admiration she was arousing. She knew that feeling and knew its signs, and saw them in Anna: saw the quivering, flashing brightness in her eyes, and the smile of happiness and excitement that curved her lips in spite of herself, and the distinct grace, sureness and lightness of her movements.

“Who is it?” she asked herself. “All of them, or one?” And, not helping the tormented young man with whom she was dancing in the conversation, whose thread he had dropped and could not pick up, and outwardly submitting to the loud, cheerful, commanding shouts of Korsunsky, who threw everyone now into the grand rond, now into the chaîne, she watched, and her heart contracted more and more. “No, it is not the admiration of the crowd that has made her drunk, but the rapture of one. And that one? Can it be he?” Every time he spoke to Anna, a joyful brightness flashed in her eyes, and a smile of happiness curved her red lips. She seemed to be making an effort over herself not to show these signs of joy, but they came out on her face of themselves. “But what of him?” Kitty looked at him and was horrified. What Kitty had seen so clearly in the mirror of Anna’s face, she saw in his. What had become of his always calm, firm manner and the carelessly calm expression of his face? No, now, every time he turned to her, he bent his head a little, as though wishing to fall down before her, and in his look there was only an expression of submission and fear. “I do not want to offend,” his look seemed to say each time, “but I want to save myself, and I don’t know how.” There was an expression on his face she had never seen before.

They talked about common acquaintances, carried on the most trifling conversation, but it seemed to Kitty that every word they said was deciding their fate and hers. And the strange thing was that though they really were talking about how ridiculous Ivan Ivanovich was with his French, and about how a better match could have been found for the Eletskaya girl, yet these words had a meaning for them, and they felt it, just as Kitty did. The whole ball, the whole world, everything was covered with mist in Kitty’s soul. Only the strict school of upbringing she had been through held her up and made her do what was required of her, that is, dance, answer questions, talk, even smile. But before the mazurka began, when they were already setting out the chairs and some couples were moving from the small rooms into the ballroom, a moment of despair and horror came over Kitty. She had refused five men, and now she was not dancing the mazurka. There was not even any hope of being asked, precisely because she had had too great a success in society, and it could not enter anyone’s head that she had not been asked before now. She ought to tell her mother she was ill and go home, but she had not the strength for that. She felt crushed.

She went to the far end of the little drawing-room and sank into an armchair. The airy skirt of her dress rose like a cloud round her slender waist; one bare, thin, tender girlish arm, hanging down helplessly, sank in the folds of her pink tunic; in the other she held her fan and with quick, short movements fanned her hot face. But in spite of this look of a butterfly that has just clung to a blade of grass and is about to flutter up and spread its rainbow wings, a terrible despair wrung her heart. “But perhaps I am mistaken; perhaps it was not so?”
And again she went over everything she had seen.
“Kitty, what does this mean?” said Countess Nordston, who had come up to her noiselessly over the carpet. “I don’t understand it.”
Kitty’s lower lip trembled; she got up quickly.
“Kitty, you are not dancing the mazurka?”
“No, no,” said Kitty in a voice trembling with tears.
“He asked her for the mazurka in front of me,” said Countess Nordston, knowing that Kitty would understand who he and she were. “She said: aren’t you dancing with Princess Shcherbatskaya?”
“Oh, it’s all the same to me!” answered Kitty.
No one but she herself understood her position; no one knew that the day before she had refused a man whom she perhaps loved, and refused him because she believed in another.
Countess Nordston found Korsunsky, with whom she was dancing the mazurka, and told him to ask Kitty.

Kitty danced in the first couple, and, luckily for her, she did not have to talk, because Korsunsky was running about all the time, directing his domain. Vronsky and Anna were sitting almost opposite her. She saw them with her long-sighted eyes, she saw them close to when they met in the figures, and the more she saw of them, the more convinced she became that her unhappiness had come to pass. She saw that they felt themselves alone in this crowded room. And on Vronsky’s face, always so firm and independent, she saw that expression which had struck her, of bewilderment and submission, like the expression of an intelligent dog when it has done wrong.

Anna smiled, and the smile passed to him. She grew thoughtful, and he became serious. Some supernatural force drew Kitty’s eyes to Anna’s face. She was lovely in her simple black dress; lovely were her full arms with their bracelets; lovely her firm neck with its string of pearls; lovely the curling hair of her disordered coiffure; lovely the graceful, light movements of her small feet and hands; lovely that beautiful face in its animation; but there was something terrible and cruel in her loveliness.

Kitty admired her still more than before, and suffered more and more. Kitty felt crushed, and her face expressed it. When Vronsky saw her, meeting her in the mazurka, he did not recognize her at once, she had changed so.
“A splendid ball!” he said to her, for the sake of saying something.
“Yes,” she answered.

In the middle of the mazurka, repeating a complicated figure newly invented by Korsunsky, Anna came out into the middle of the circle, took two partners, and called a lady and Kitty to her. Kitty looked at her in fright as she came up. Anna looked at her with half-closed eyes and smiled, pressing her hand. But, noticing that Kitty’s face answered her smile only with an expression of despair and surprise, she turned away from her and began talking gaily to the other lady.
“Yes, there is something terrible, devilish and lovely in her,” Kitty said to herself.
Anna did not want to stay for supper, but the host began to press her.
“Come now, Anna Arkadyevna,” Korsunsky began, drawing her bare arm under the sleeve of his tailcoat. “What an idea I have for the cotillion! Un bijou!”
And he moved little by little, trying to draw her along. The host smiled approvingly.
“No, I shall not stay,” answered Anna, smiling; but in spite of the smile, both Korsunsky and the host understood from the decided tone in which she answered that she would not stay.
“No, as it is I have danced more in Moscow at your one ball than all winter in Petersburg,” said Anna, glancing round at Vronsky, who was standing beside her. “I must rest before the journey.”
“And you are really going tomorrow?” asked Vronsky.
“Yes, I think so,” answered Anna, as though surprised at the boldness of his question; but the irrepressible quivering brightness of her eyes and of her smile scorched him as she said it.
Anna Arkadyevna did not stay for supper, and left.
## Chapter XXIV

“Yes, there is something repulsive about me, something that pushes people away,” thought Levin, as he left the Shcherbatskys’ and set off on foot to his brother’s. “And I am no good for other people. Pride, they say. No, I haven’t even any pride. If I had pride, I would not have put myself in such a position.” And he pictured to himself Vronsky, happy, kind, clever and calm, who had surely never been in the terrible position he had been in that evening. “Yes, she was bound to choose him. That is how it must be, and I have no one to complain of, and nothing to complain about. I am to blame myself. What right had I to think that she would want to join her life to mine? Who am I? And what am I? A nonentity, needed by no one and for nothing.” And he remembered his brother Nikolai and dwelt on the memory with joy. “Isn’t he right that everything in the world is bad and vile? And I doubt that we judge, or have judged, brother Nikolai fairly. Of course, from the point of view of Prokofy, who saw him in a torn fur coat and drunk, he is a contemptible man; but I know him differently. I know his soul, and I know that he and I are alike. And instead of going to find him, I went out to dine, and came here.” Levin went up to a street-lamp, read his brother’s address, which he had in his pocket-book, and called a cab. All the long way to his brother’s Levin vividly recalled all the events of brother Nikolai’s life that he knew. He remembered how his brother, at the university and for a year after the university, in spite of his comrades’ mockery, had lived like a monk, strictly observing all the rites of religion, the services, the fasts, and avoiding every pleasure, especially women; and then how he had suddenly broken loose, taken up with the vilest people and plunged into the most dissolute debauchery. He remembered then the business of the boy whom he had taken from the country to bring up, and, in a fit of fury, beaten so badly that proceedings were started against him for causing injury. He remembered then the business of the card-sharper to whom he had lost money, given a promissory note, and against whom he had himself brought a complaint, trying to prove that the man had cheated him. (That was the money Sergei Ivanych had paid.) Then he remembered how he had spent a night in the police station for disorderly conduct. He remembered the shameful lawsuit he had started against his brother Sergei Ivanych, for supposedly not having paid him his share of their mother’s estate; and the last affair, when he had gone to take up a post in the Western Region and had been brought to trial there for beating a village elder… It was all terribly vile, but to Levin it did not seem nearly as vile as it must have seemed to those who did not know Nikolai Levin, did not know his whole story, did not know his heart.

Levin remembered how, at the time when Nikolai was in his period of piety, of fasts, monks and church services, when he was seeking in religion a help, a bridle for his passionate nature, not only had no one supported him, but everyone, Levin himself included, had laughed at him. They had teased him, called him Noah, the monk; and when he broke loose, no one had helped him, but everyone had turned away with horror and disgust.

Levin felt that his brother Nikolai, in his soul, in the very foundation of his soul, in spite of all the ugliness of his life, was no more in the wrong than the people who despised him. He was not to blame for having been born with his unrestrainable character and a mind somehow cramped. But he had always wanted to be good. “I will tell him everything, I will make him tell me everything, and I will show him that I love him and so understand him,” Levin decided to himself, as he drove up, after ten o’clock, to the hotel named in the address.
“Upstairs, numbers 12 and 13,” the porter answered Levin’s question.
“Is he in?”
“He must be.”

The door of number 12 was half open, and from it, in a strip of light, came the thick smoke of bad, weak tobacco, and a voice unknown to Levin could be heard; but Levin knew at once that his brother was there: he heard his cough.
As he came in at the door, the unknown voice was saying:
“Everything depends on how reasonably and consciously the thing is carried on.”

Konstantin Levin looked in at the door and saw that the speaker was a young man with an enormous shock of hair, in a peasant’s coat, while a young pock-marked woman in a woollen dress without cuffs or collar was sitting on the sofa. His brother could not be seen. Konstantin’s heart contracted painfully at the thought of the strange people among whom his brother was living. No one heard him, and Konstantin, taking off his galoshes, listened to what the gentleman in the peasant coat was saying. He was talking about some enterprise.
“Well, the devil take them, the privileged classes,” his brother’s voice said, clearing his throat. “Masha! Get us some supper and give us some wine, if there’s any left; otherwise send out for it.”
The woman got up, went behind the partition and saw Konstantin.
“There’s some gentleman, Nikolai Dmitrich,” she said.
“Who does he want?” said Nikolai Levin’s voice angrily.
“It’s me,” answered Konstantin Levin, coming out into the light.

“Who’s me?” Nikolai’s voice repeated, still more angrily. He could be heard getting up quickly, catching against something, and Levin saw before him in the doorway the enormous, thin, stooping figure of his brother, so familiar and yet so startling in its wildness and sickliness, with his big frightened eyes.

He was still thinner than three years before, when Konstantin Levin had seen him last. He was wearing a short frock-coat. And his hands and broad bones seemed still more enormous. His hair had grown thinner; the same straight moustache hung over his lips; the same eyes looked strangely and naively at the newcomer.

“Ah, Kostya!” he said suddenly, recognizing his brother, and his eyes lit up with joy. But in that same second he looked round at the young man and made that convulsive movement of his head and neck, so familiar to Konstantin, as though his tie were choking him; and quite another expression, wild, suffering and cruel, settled on his emaciated face.
“I wrote to you and to Sergei Ivanych that I don’t know you and don’t want to know you. What do you, what do you want?”

He was not at all as Konstantin had imagined him. The hardest and worst thing in his character, what made it so difficult to have anything to do with him, had been forgotten by Konstantin Levin when he thought of him; and now, when he saw his face, and especially that convulsive turning of the head, he remembered it all.
“I don’t need to see you for anything,” he answered timidly. “I simply came to see you.”
His brother’s timidity evidently softened Nikolai. His lips twitched.

“Ah, is that it?” he said. “Well, come in, sit down. Do you want some supper? Masha, bring three portions. No, wait. Do you know who this is?” he said to his brother, pointing to the gentleman in the peasant coat. “This is Mr Kritsky, my friend from Kiev days, a very remarkable man. The police persecute him, of course, because he is not a scoundrel.”

And he looked round, from habit, at everyone in the room. Seeing that the woman standing in the doorway was about to go, he shouted to her: “Wait, I said.” And with that inability, that clumsiness in conversation, which Konstantin knew so well, he began, again looking round at everyone, to tell his brother Kritsky’s story: how he had been expelled from the university because he had started a society for helping poor students, and Sunday schools; and how he had afterwards become a teacher in a village school, and how he had been driven out of there too; and how he had then been tried for something.
“You were at Kiev University?” Konstantin Levin said to Kritsky, to break the awkward silence that had set in.
“Yes, Kiev,” said Kritsky angrily, scowling.

“And this woman,” Nikolai Levin interrupted him, pointing to her, “is the companion of my life, Marya Nikolaevna. I took her out of a house,” and his neck jerked as he said it. “But I love her and respect her, and all who want to know me,” he added, raising his voice and frowning, “I ask to love and respect her. She is the same as my wife, just the same. So now you know whom you are dealing with. And if you think you will be lowering yourself, there is God, and there is the door.”
And again his eyes ran questioningly over everyone.
“Why should I be lowering myself? I don’t understand.”
“Then, Masha, have them bring supper: three portions, vodka and wine… No, wait… No, never mind… Go.”
## Part Two · Chapter XXV

Seventeen officers in all were riding. The race was to be run on the big elliptical course, nearly three miles round, in front of the pavilion. Nine obstacles had been set up on this course: the river; a big solid barrier, nearly five feet high, right in front of the pavilion; a dry ditch; a ditch with water; a steep slope; an Irish bank, which was one of the hardest obstacles, consisting of a mound stuck with brushwood, behind which, invisible to the horse, there was another ditch, so that the horse had to clear both obstacles or kill itself; then two more ditches with water and one dry one; and the finish was opposite the pavilion. But the race did not start on the course; it started some two hundred yards to one side of it, and on that stretch was the first obstacle, a dammed river seven feet wide, which the riders could jump or ford as they chose.

Three times or so the riders were brought into line, but each time someone’s horse pushed forward, and they had to go back and begin again. The expert starter, Colonel Sestrin, was already beginning to get angry when at last, the fourth time, he shouted “Go!” and the riders set off.
All eyes, all field-glasses, were turned on the bright little cluster of riders while they were being lined up.
“They’re off! They’re racing!” was heard from all sides after the silence of waiting.

And groups and solitary walkers began running from place to place to see better. In the very first minute the bunched-up cluster of riders drew out, and one could see them approaching the river in twos and threes and one behind another. To the spectators it seemed that they had all started together; but for the riders there were seconds of difference that meant a great deal to them.

Frou-Frou, excited and over-nervous, lost the first moment, and several horses got off before her; but before they reached the river Vronsky, holding back with all his strength the horse, which was pulling on the reins, easily passed three of them, and in front of him there remained only Makhotin’s chestnut Gladiator, whose hindquarters rose and fell evenly and lightly just in front of Vronsky, and, ahead of everyone, the lovely Diana, carrying Kuzovlev, more dead than alive.
In the first minutes Vronsky was master neither of himself nor of his horse. Until the first obstacle, the river, he could not direct the horse’s movements.

Gladiator and Diana came up to it together and almost at the same moment: one, two, they rose over the river and flew across to the other side; imperceptibly, as if flying, Frou-Frou soared up after them; but at the very moment when Vronsky felt himself in the air, he suddenly saw, almost under his horse’s feet, Kuzovlev floundering with Diana on the other side of the river (Kuzovlev had let go of the reins after the jump, and the horse had gone head over heels with him). These details Vronsky learned only afterwards; now he saw only that just where Frou-Frou must land, Diana’s leg or head might be in the way. But Frou-Frou, like a falling cat, made an effort with her legs and back in the middle of the jump and, clearing the other horse, raced on.
“Oh, you darling!” thought Vronsky.

After the river Vronsky had complete mastery of his horse, and began to hold her back, meaning to take the big barrier behind Makhotin and then, on the following stretch of some four hundred yards without obstacles, to try to pass him.

The big barrier stood right in front of the Imperial pavilion. The Emperor, and the whole court, and crowds of people, all were looking at them, at him and at Makhotin a length ahead of him, as they came up to “the devil” (as the solid barrier was called). Vronsky felt these eyes turned on him from all sides, but he saw nothing except the ears and neck of his horse, the ground running towards him, and the hindquarters and white legs of Gladiator, quickly beating time in front of him and staying always the same distance away. Gladiator rose without touching anything, flicked his short tail, and vanished from Vronsky’s sight.
“Bravo!” said a single voice.

At that same instant the planks of the barrier flashed before Vronsky’s eyes, right in front of him. Without the slightest change in her movement the horse soared up under him; the planks disappeared, and only something knocked behind. Excited by Gladiator going ahead, the horse had risen too early before the barrier and struck it with a hind hoof. But her pace did not change, and Vronsky, getting a lump of mud in his face, understood that he was again the same distance behind Gladiator. Again he saw ahead of him his hindquarters, his short tail, and again those same quickly moving white legs that came no nearer.

At the very instant when Vronsky thought that now he must pass Makhotin, Frou-Frou herself, understanding what he had thought, without any urging, put on speed considerably and began closing on Makhotin on the most favourable side, the side of the rope. Makhotin would not give up the rope. Vronsky had only thought that he could also pass on the outside, when Frou-Frou changed her leg and began passing in just that way. Frou-Frou’s shoulder, already beginning to darken with sweat, came level with Gladiator’s hindquarters. For a few strides they went side by side. But before the obstacle they were coming to, Vronsky, so as not to take the wide circle, began working the reins, and quickly, on the very slope, passed Makhotin. He caught a glimpse of his face, spattered with mud. It even seemed to him that he smiled. Vronsky had passed Makhotin, but he felt him right behind him, and never stopped hearing at his very back the even stride and the abrupt, still quite fresh breathing of Gladiator’s nostrils.

The next two obstacles, a ditch and a barrier, were taken easily, but Vronsky began to hear Gladiator’s snorting and stride closer. He urged on his horse, and felt with joy that she easily increased her pace, and the sound of Gladiator’s hoofs was heard again at the same distance as before.

Vronsky was leading the race, which was just what he had wanted to do and what Cord had advised him, and now he was sure of success. His excitement, his joy and his tenderness for Frou-Frou grew stronger and stronger. He longed to look round, but he did not dare, and tried to calm himself and not to urge his horse, so as to keep in her a reserve equal to the one he felt was left in Gladiator. There remained one obstacle, and the hardest; if he cleared it ahead of the others, he would come in first. He was galloping up to the Irish bank. Together with Frou-Frou he saw this bank from far off, and to both of them, to him and the horse, came a momentary doubt. He noticed hesitation in the horse’s ears and raised his whip, but at once felt that the doubt was groundless: the horse knew what was needed. She put on speed and, evenly, just as he had expected, soared up, and, pushing off from the ground, gave herself up to the force of her momentum, which carried her far over the ditch; and in the same rhythm, without effort, on the same leg, Frou-Frou went on with the race.

“Bravo, Vronsky!” he heard the voices of a group of people, men of his regiment and friends, he knew, who were standing at this obstacle; he could not fail to recognize Yashvin’s voice, but he did not see him.

“Oh, my beauty!” he thought of Frou-Frou, listening to what was happening behind. “He’s over!” he thought, hearing Gladiator’s stride behind him. There remained one last little ditch with water, five feet wide; Vronsky did not even look at it, but, wanting to come in a long way first, began working the reins in a circular motion, raising and lowering the horse’s head in time with her stride. He felt that the horse was going on her last reserve; not only her neck and shoulders were wet, but on her withers, her head, her sharp ears the sweat stood out in drops, and she was breathing sharply and shortly. But he knew that this reserve was more than enough for the remaining four hundred yards. Only because he felt himself closer to the ground, and from the special smoothness of her movement, did Vronsky know how much his horse had increased her speed. She flew over the little ditch as if not noticing it. She flew over it like a bird; but at that very moment Vronsky, to his horror, felt that, failing to keep up with the horse’s movement, he had, not understanding how himself, made a bad, unforgivable movement, letting himself down into the saddle. Suddenly his position changed, and he understood that something terrible had happened. He could not yet give himself an account of what had happened, when the white legs of the chestnut stallion flashed right beside him, and Makhotin went past at a fast gallop. Vronsky was touching the ground with one foot, and his horse was falling over on that foot. He just managed to free his leg as she fell on one side, wheezing heavily, and, making vain efforts with her slender, sweating neck to get up, she fluttered on the ground at his feet like a shot bird. The clumsy movement Vronsky had made had broken her back. But that he understood much later. Now he saw only that Makhotin was quickly moving away, while he stood alone, staggering, on the muddy, motionless ground, and before him, breathing heavily, lay Frou-Frou, who, bending her head towards him, looked at him with her lovely eye. Still not understanding what had happened, Vronsky pulled at the horse’s rein. Again she struggled all over, like a fish, creaking the flaps of the saddle, freed her front legs, but, unable to lift her hindquarters, at once began to tremble and fell on her side again. His face disfigured with passion, pale, his lower jaw shaking, Vronsky struck her in the belly with his heel and again began pulling at the reins. But she did not move, and, burying her muzzle in the ground, only looked at her master with her speaking eyes.

“Aaah!” groaned Vronsky, clutching his head. “Aaah! What have I done!” he cried. “And the race lost! And my own fault, shameful, unforgivable! And this poor, dear, ruined horse! Aaah! What have I done!”

People, a doctor and his assistant, officers of his regiment, were running towards him. To his misfortune, he felt that he was whole and unhurt. The horse had broken her back, and it was decided to shoot her. Vronsky could not answer questions, could not speak to anyone. He turned and, without picking up the cap that had fallen off his head, walked away from the racecourse, not knowing himself where he was going. He felt wretched. For the first time in his life he had experienced the heaviest kind of misfortune, a misfortune that could not be put right, and one for which he himself was to blame.

Yashvin caught up with him with his cap and took him home, and in half an hour Vronsky came to himself. But the memory of this race stayed in his soul for a long time as the heaviest and most tormenting memory of his life.
## Chapter XXVI

Outwardly the relations of Alexei Alexandrovich with his wife were the same as before. The only difference was that he was even busier than before. As in former years, at the opening of spring he went abroad to a spa to restore his health, which was upset every year by his intensive winter work, and, as usual, he came back in July and at once took up his usual work with increased energy. As usual, his wife had moved to their summer villa, while he stayed in Petersburg.

Since that conversation after the evening at Princess Tverskaya’s he had never spoken to Anna of his suspicions and jealousy, and that habitual tone of his, as of someone mimicking somebody, could not have been more convenient for his present relations with his wife. He was somewhat colder to his wife. He seemed only to have a slight grudge against her for that first night-time conversation, which she had put aside. In his attitude to her there was a shade of vexation, but no more. “You did not want to have it out with me,” he seemed to say, addressing her in his mind; “so much the worse for you. Now you will have to ask me, and I shall not have it out. So much the worse for you,” he said in his mind, like a man who has vainly tried to put out a fire, become angry at his vain efforts, and said: “Well then, take that! You shall burn for this!”

He, this man so clever and subtle in the affairs of his service, did not understand the whole madness of such an attitude to his wife. He did not understand it because it was too frightening for him to understand his real position, and in his soul he had closed, locked and sealed that drawer in which he kept his feelings for his family, that is, for his wife and son. He, an attentive father, had become particularly cold to his son since the end of that winter, and had the same bantering manner with him as with his wife. “Ah! young man!” he would address him.

Alexei Alexandrovich thought and said that in no year had he had so much official work as this one; but he was not aware that he himself was inventing work for himself this year, that it was one of the means of not opening that drawer where his feelings for his wife and family and his thoughts about them lay, and which became more frightening the longer they lay there. If anyone had had the right to ask Alexei Alexandrovich what he thought of his wife’s behaviour, the mild, meek Alexei Alexandrovich would have answered nothing, but would have been very angry with the man who asked him about it. That is why there was something proud and stern in the expression of Alexei Alexandrovich’s face when he was asked about his wife’s health. Alexei Alexandrovich did not want to think anything about his wife’s behaviour and feelings, and indeed he did not think anything about them.

Alexei Alexandrovich’s regular summer villa was in Peterhof, and usually Countess Lidia Ivanovna lived there in the summer too, as Anna’s neighbour and in constant contact with her. This year Countess Lidia Ivanovna had refused to live in Peterhof, had not once been to see Anna Arkadyevna, and had hinted to Alexei Alexandrovich that Anna’s intimacy with Betsy and Vronsky was unsuitable. Alexei Alexandrovich had stopped her sternly, expressing the thought that his wife was above suspicion, and since then he had begun to avoid Countess Lidia Ivanovna. He did not want to see, and did not see, that many people in society were already looking askance at his wife; he did not want to understand, and did not understand, why his wife had particularly insisted on moving to Tsarskoe, where Betsy lived, and from which it was not far to the camp of Vronsky’s regiment. He did not allow himself to think about it, and did not think; yet at the same time, in the depths of his soul, never putting it into words to himself and having not only no proofs of it but no suspicions either, he knew beyond doubt that he was a deceived husband, and was deeply unhappy because of it.

How many times in the course of his eight years of happy life with his wife, looking at other men’s unfaithful wives and deceived husbands, had Alexei Alexandrovich said to himself: “How can anyone let it come to that? How can anyone not untie such an ugly situation?” But now, when the trouble had fallen on his own head, not only did he not think of how to untie the situation, he did not want to know of it at all, did not want to know precisely because it was too terrible, too unnatural.

Since his return from abroad Alexei Alexandrovich had been to the villa twice. Once he dined, and another time he spent the evening with guests, but not once did he stay the night, as he had been in the habit of doing in former years.

The day of the races was a very busy day for Alexei Alexandrovich; but, having drawn up a timetable for the day early in the morning, he decided that immediately after an early dinner he would drive to his wife at the villa and from there to the races, at which the whole court would be present and at which he had to be. He would call on his wife because he had decided to visit her once a week for the sake of appearances. Besides, on that day he had to hand his wife money for her expenses, as was the established custom, by the fifteenth of the month.
With his usual control over his thoughts, having thought all this out about his wife, he did not allow his thoughts to range further over what concerned her.

That morning was a very busy one for Alexei Alexandrovich. The evening before, Countess Lidia Ivanovna had sent him a pamphlet by a famous traveller in China who was in Petersburg, with a letter asking him to receive the traveller himself, a man who for various reasons was very interesting and useful. Alexei Alexandrovich had not had time to read the pamphlet in the evening and finished it in the morning. Then petitioners came, and there began reports, receptions, appointments, dismissals, distributions of awards, pensions, salaries, correspondence: that workaday business, as Alexei Alexandrovich called it, which took up so much time. Then there was private business, a visit from the doctor and from his steward. The steward did not take much time. He only handed over the money Alexei Alexandrovich needed and gave a brief report on the state of his affairs, which were not altogether good, since it so happened that this year, because of frequent outings, more had been spent and there was a deficit. But the doctor, a famous Petersburg doctor who was on friendly terms with Alexei Alexandrovich, took up a great deal of time. Alexei Alexandrovich had not been expecting him that day and was surprised by his visit, and still more by the doctor’s questioning Alexei Alexandrovich very attentively about his condition, listening to his chest, tapping and feeling his liver. Alexei Alexandrovich did not know that his friend Lidia Ivanovna, noticing that Alexei Alexandrovich’s health was not good this year, had asked the doctor to come and look at the patient. “Do it for my sake,” Countess Lidia Ivanovna had said to him.
“I shall do it for Russia’s sake, Countess,” the doctor had answered.
“A priceless man!” Countess Lidia Ivanovna had said.

The doctor was very dissatisfied with Alexei Alexandrovich. He found the liver considerably enlarged, the nourishment reduced, and no effect at all from the waters. He prescribed as much physical exercise as possible and as little mental strain as possible, and above all no distress of any kind: that is, the very thing that was as impossible for Alexei Alexandrovich as not breathing; and he left, leaving in Alexei Alexandrovich an unpleasant awareness that something was wrong with him and that it could not be put right.

Coming out from Alexei Alexandrovich, the doctor ran into Slyudin on the porch, Alexei Alexandrovich’s head of chancery, whom he knew well. They had been fellow students at the university and, though they met rarely, they respected each other and were good friends; and so there was no one to whom the doctor would have spoken his frank opinion of the patient as he would to Slyudin.
“How glad I am that you have seen him,” said Slyudin. “He is not well, it seems to me… Well, what is it?”

“This is what,” said the doctor, waving over Slyudin’s head to his coachman to bring the carriage round. “This is what,” said the doctor, taking a finger of his kid glove in his white hands and pulling it tight. “If you don’t stretch a string and try to break it, it is very hard; but stretch it to the last limit and press on the stretched string with the weight of a finger, and it snaps. And he, with his assiduity, his conscientiousness about his work, he is stretched to the utmost degree; and there is pressure from outside, and a heavy one,” the doctor concluded, raising his eyebrows significantly. “Will you be at the races?” he added, going down to the waiting carriage. “Yes, yes, of course, it takes a great deal of time,” the doctor answered something to what Slyudin had said and he had not caught.

After the doctor, who had taken up so much time, came the famous traveller, and Alexei Alexandrovich, making use of the pamphlet he had just read and of his earlier knowledge of the subject, struck the traveller with the depth of his knowledge of it and the breadth of his enlightened outlook.

Together with the traveller, the arrival of a provincial marshal of nobility was announced, who had come to Petersburg and with whom it was necessary to have a talk. After he had gone it was necessary to finish the workaday business with the head of chancery, and there was still a call to be made on a serious and important matter on a certain important person. Alexei Alexandrovich only just managed to get back by five o’clock, his dinner hour, and, having dined with the head of chancery, he invited him to drive with him to the villa and to the races.
Without admitting it to himself, Alexei Alexandrovich was now looking for opportunities to have a third person present at his meetings with his wife.
## Chapter XXVII
Anna was standing upstairs in front of the mirror, pinning the last bow on her dress with Annushka’s help, when she heard by the porch the sound of wheels crunching the gravel.

“It’s too early for Betsy,” she thought, and, looking out of the window, she saw the carriage and, leaning out of it, a black hat and the so familiar ears of Alexei Alexandrovich. “How inconvenient: can he be going to stay the night?” she thought. And everything that might come of it seemed to her so terrible and frightening that, without a moment’s thought, with a gay and radiant face, she went out to meet them, and, feeling within her the presence of the spirit of lies and deceit, already familiar to her, she at once gave herself up to this spirit and began talking, not knowing herself what she would say.

“Ah, how nice of you!” she said, giving her husband her hand and greeting Slyudin, who was like one of the household, with a smile. “You’ll stay the night, I hope?” was the first word the spirit of deceit prompted her with. “And now we’ll go together. Only it’s a pity I promised Betsy. She is calling for me.”
Alexei Alexandrovich frowned at the name of Betsy.

“Oh, I shall not separate the inseparables,” he said in his usual joking tone. “Mikhail Vasilyevich and I will go. The doctors tell me to walk, too. I shall stroll along the way and imagine that I am at the spa.”
“There is no hurry,” said Anna. “Will you have some tea?” She rang.

“Bring tea, and tell Seryozha that Alexei Alexandrovich has come. Well, and how is your health? Mikhail Vasilyevich, you have never been to see me; look how nice it is on my balcony,” she said, turning now to one, now to the other.

She spoke very simply and naturally, but too much and too fast. She felt this herself, all the more because in the curious glance Mikhail Vasilyevich gave her she noticed that he seemed to be watching her.
Mikhail Vasilyevich at once went out onto the terrace.
She sat down beside her husband.
“You don’t look quite well,” she said.
“Yes,” he said; “the doctor was with me today and took up an hour of my time. I feel that one of my friends sent him: so precious is my health…”
“No, but what did he say?”
She asked him about his health and his work, urged him to rest and to move out to her.

All this she said gaily, quickly, and with a special brightness in her eyes; but Alexei Alexandrovich now attached no significance to her tone. He heard only her words and gave them only their direct meaning. And he answered her simply, though jokingly. There was nothing special in the whole conversation, but never afterwards could Anna remember this whole short scene without a tormenting pain of shame.

Seryozha came in, preceded by his governess. If Alexei Alexandrovich had allowed himself to observe, he would have noticed the timid, bewildered look with which Seryozha glanced at his father and then at his mother. But he did not want to see anything, and he did not see.
“Ah, young man! He has grown. Really, he is becoming quite a man. Good day, young man.”
And he gave his hand to the frightened Seryozha.

Seryozha, who had been shy of his father before, now, since Alexei Alexandrovich had begun calling him young man, and since the riddle of whether Vronsky was friend or enemy had come into his head, kept away from his father. He looked round at his mother, as though asking for protection. Only with his mother was he happy. Meanwhile Alexei Alexandrovich, having started talking to the governess, was holding his son by the shoulder, and Seryozha felt so tormentingly awkward that Anna saw he was about to cry.

Anna, who had blushed the moment her son came in, noticing that Seryozha was ill at ease, jumped up quickly, lifted Alexei Alexandrovich’s hand from her son’s shoulder, and, kissing her son, led him out onto the terrace and came back at once.
“But it’s time to go,” she said, looking at her watch. “Why doesn’t Betsy come!…”

“Yes,” said Alexei Alexandrovich, and, getting up, he clasped his hands and cracked his fingers. “I came also to bring you money, since nightingales are not fed on fables,” he said. “You need it, I expect.”
“No, I don’t… yes, I do,” she said, not looking at him and blushing to the roots of her hair. “But you will call in here after the races, I expect.”

“Oh yes!” answered Alexei Alexandrovich. “And here is the beauty of Peterhof, Princess Tverskaya,” he added, looking out of the window at an English carriage with blinkered horses and a tiny body set extremely high, which was driving up. “What elegance! Charming! Well then, let us be going too.”
Princess Tverskaya did not get out of the carriage; only her footman, in gaiters, a short cape and a black hat, jumped down at the porch.
“I’m going, goodbye!” said Anna, and, kissing her son, she went up to Alexei Alexandrovich and held out her hand to him. “It was very nice of you to come.”
Alexei Alexandrovich kissed her hand.

“Well, goodbye then. You’ll come in for tea, splendid!” she said, and went out, radiant and gay. But as soon as she could no longer see him, she felt the place on her hand that his lips had touched, and shuddered with disgust.
## Chapter XXVIII

When Alexei Alexandrovich appeared at the races, Anna was already sitting in the pavilion beside Betsy, the pavilion where all high society gathered. She saw her husband from far off. Two men, her husband and her lover, were the two centres of her life, and without the help of her outward senses she felt their nearness. She felt her husband’s approach while he was still far off, and could not help following him with her eyes in the waves of the crowd through which he was moving. She saw how he came towards the pavilion, now condescendingly answering ingratiating bows, now greeting his equals in a friendly, absent-minded way, now carefully waiting for a glance from the great of this world and raising his big round hat, which pressed on the tips of his ears. She knew all these ways of his, and all of them were loathsome to her. “Nothing but ambition, nothing but the wish to succeed, that is all there is in his soul,” she thought; “and lofty considerations, love of enlightenment, religion, all that is only a tool for succeeding.”

From his glances at the ladies’ pavilion (he was looking straight at her but did not recognize his wife in the sea of muslin, tulle, ribbons, hair and parasols) she understood that he was looking for her; but she deliberately did not notice him.
“Alexei Alexandrovich!” Princess Betsy called to him. “You can’t see your wife, I expect; here she is!”
He smiled his cold smile.

“There is so much brilliance here that one’s eyes are dazzled,” he said, and went into the pavilion. He smiled at his wife as a husband ought to smile on meeting a wife he has only just seen, and greeted the princess and other acquaintances, giving each his due, that is, joking with the ladies and exchanging greetings with the men. Below, beside the pavilion, stood an adjutant-general whom Alexei Alexandrovich respected, known for his intelligence and education. Alexei Alexandrovich began talking with him.

There was an interval between races, and so nothing hindered conversation. The adjutant-general was condemning races. Alexei Alexandrovich was objecting, defending them. Anna listened to his thin, even voice, not missing a single word, and every word of his seemed false to her and cut her ear with pain.

When the steeplechase of nearly three miles began, she bent forward and, never taking her eyes away, watched Vronsky going up to his horse and mounting, and at the same time heard that loathsome, never-ceasing voice of her husband. She was tormented with fear for Vronsky, but still more tormented by what seemed to her the never-ceasing sound of her husband’s thin voice with its familiar intonations.

“I am a bad woman, I am a ruined woman,” she thought, “but I don’t like lying, I can’t bear lies, and his food is lies. He knows everything, sees everything; what can he feel, if he can talk so calmly? If he killed me, if he killed Vronsky, I would respect him. But no, all he needs is lies and propriety,” Anna said to herself, not thinking of what exactly she wanted from her husband, what she would have liked him to be. Nor did she understand that this particular talkativeness of Alexei Alexandrovich today, which so irritated her, was only the expression of his inner alarm and uneasiness. As a child who has hurt himself jumps about, setting his muscles moving to deaden the pain, so for Alexei Alexandrovich mental movement was necessary to deaden those thoughts about his wife which, in her presence and in Vronsky’s, and with the constant repetition of his name, demanded attention. And as it is natural for a child to jump, so it was natural for him to talk well and cleverly. He was saying:

“Danger in races of military men and cavalrymen is an essential condition of racing. If England can point in her military history to the most brilliant cavalry feats, it is only thanks to her having historically developed this strength in animals and men. Sport, in my opinion, has great significance, and, as always, we see only what is most superficial.”
“Not superficial,” said Princess Tverskaya. “One officer, they say, has broken two ribs.”
Alexei Alexandrovich smiled his smile, which only showed his teeth and said nothing more.

“Let us grant, Princess, that this is not superficial,” he said, “but internal. But that is not the point,” and he turned again to the general, with whom he was talking seriously. “Do not forget that it is military men who are racing, who have chosen this activity, and you will agree that every calling has its other side of the medal. This forms a direct part of a military man’s duties. The ugly sport of prize-fighting or of Spanish toreadors is a sign of barbarism. But specialized sport is a sign of development.”
“No, I shan’t come another time; it excites me too much,” said Princess Betsy. “Isn’t that so, Anna?”
“It excites one, but one can’t tear oneself away,” said another lady. “If I had been a Roman woman, I wouldn’t have missed a single circus.”
Anna said nothing and, not lowering her field-glass, looked at one spot.
At that moment a tall general was passing through the pavilion. Breaking off his speech, Alexei Alexandrovich got up hurriedly but with dignity, and bowed low to the passing officer.
“You are not racing?” the officer joked to him.
“My race is a harder one,” Alexei Alexandrovich answered respectfully.
And although the answer meant nothing, the officer looked as if he had received a witty saying from a witty man and fully understood la pointe de la sauce.

“There are two sides,” Alexei Alexandrovich went on, sitting down, “the performers and the spectators; and love of these spectacles is the surest sign of low development in the spectators, I agree, but…”
“Princess, a bet!” Stepan Arkadyich’s voice was heard from below, addressing Betsy. “Whom are you backing?”
“Anna and I are for Prince Kuzovlev,” answered Betsy.
“I’m for Vronsky. A pair of gloves.”
“Done!”
“How beautiful it is, isn’t it?”
Alexei Alexandrovich was silent while people around him talked, but at once began again.
“I agree, but manly games…” he was going on.

But at that moment the riders were being started, and all conversation stopped. Alexei Alexandrovich fell silent, and everyone got up and turned towards the river. Alexei Alexandrovich was not interested in races and so did not look at the riders, but began absent-mindedly letting his tired eyes wander over the spectators. His gaze stopped on Anna.

Her face was pale and stern. She evidently saw nothing and no one except one man. Her hand clutched her fan convulsively, and she was not breathing. He looked at her and hurriedly turned away, looking at other faces.

“Yes, and that lady and the others too are very excited; it is very natural,” Alexei Alexandrovich said to himself. He wanted not to look at her, but his gaze was drawn to her in spite of himself. Again he peered into that face, trying not to read what was so clearly written on it, and against his will read on it with horror what he did not want to know.

Kuzovlev’s first fall at the river excited everyone, but Alexei Alexandrovich saw clearly on Anna’s pale, triumphant face that the man she was looking at had not fallen. When, after Makhotin and Vronsky had cleared the big barrier, the next officer fell right there on his head and was killed outright, and a rustle of horror passed through the whole public, Alexei Alexandrovich saw that Anna had not even noticed it and had difficulty understanding what people around her had started talking about. But he peered at her more and more often and with greater persistence. Anna, entirely absorbed in the sight of Vronsky racing, felt from one side the gaze of her husband’s cold eyes fixed on her.
She looked round for an instant, glanced at him questioningly, and, frowning slightly, turned away again.
“Oh, I don’t care,” she seemed to say to him, and did not look at him again once.

The races were unlucky, and of the seventeen men more than half fell and were hurt. Towards the end of the races everyone was in a state of agitation, which was increased still more by the Emperor’s being displeased.
## Chapter XXIX

Everyone was expressing disapproval aloud, everyone was repeating a phrase someone had said: “All that’s missing is a circus with lions”; and horror was felt by everyone, so that when Vronsky fell and Anna gasped aloud, there was nothing unusual in it. But after that a change took place in Anna’s face that was positively improper. She lost her head completely. She began to struggle like a caught bird: now she wanted to get up and go somewhere, now she turned to Betsy.
“Let us go, let us go,” she kept saying.
But Betsy did not hear her. She was leaning over and talking to a general who had come up to her.
Alexei Alexandrovich came up to Anna and courteously offered her his arm.
“Let us go, if you wish,” he said in French; but Anna was listening to what the general was saying and did not notice her husband.
“He has broken his leg too, they say,” the general was saying. “This is beyond everything.”

Anna, without answering her husband, raised her field-glass and looked at the place where Vronsky had fallen; but it was so far, and so many people had crowded there, that nothing could be made out. She lowered the glass and was about to go; but at that moment an officer galloped up and was reporting something to the Emperor. Anna leaned forward, listening.
“Stiva! Stiva!” she called to her brother.
But her brother did not hear her. Again she was about to leave.
“I offer you my arm once more, if you wish to go,” said Alexei Alexandrovich, touching her hand.
She drew away from him with disgust and, without looking him in the face, answered:
“No, no, leave me alone, I shall stay.”
She saw now that from the place where Vronsky had fallen an officer was running across the course towards the pavilion. Betsy waved her handkerchief to him.
The officer brought the news that the rider was not hurt, but that the horse had broken its back.

Hearing this, Anna quickly sat down and covered her face with her fan. Alexei Alexandrovich saw that she was crying, and could hold back not only her tears but not even the sobs that heaved her bosom. Alexei Alexandrovich screened her with his body, giving her time to recover.
“For the third time I offer you my arm,” he said after a while, turning to her. Anna looked at him and did not know what to say. Princess Betsy came to her rescue.
“No, Alexei Alexandrovich, I brought Anna, and I promised to take her back,” Betsy put in.
“Excuse me, Princess,” he said, smiling courteously but looking her firmly in the eyes, “but I see that Anna is not quite well, and I wish her to come with me.”
Anna looked round in fright, got up submissively, and laid her hand on her husband’s arm.
“I’ll send to him, find out, and send you word,” Betsy whispered to her.

On the way out of the pavilion Alexei Alexandrovich, just as always, talked to the people he met, and Anna had, as always, to answer and talk; but she was not herself, and walked on her husband’s arm as if in a dream.
“Is he killed or not? Is it true? Will he come or not? Shall I see him today?” she thought.

In silence she got into Alexei Alexandrovich’s carriage, and in silence they drove out of the crowd of carriages. In spite of all he had seen, Alexei Alexandrovich still did not allow himself to think of his wife’s real situation. He saw only the outward signs.
